title: PREDICTING THE SPREAD OF AIRBORNE VIRAL INFECTIONS IN ENCLOSED SPACES
authors: Alibek Issakhov, A. Akylbekkyzy, Aizhan Abylkassymova
abstract: The spread of respiratory viral infections in enclosed spaces remains one of the most serious threats to public health in the 21st century. The SARS and MERS epidemics, along with the COVID-19 pandemic, have demonstrated the high vulnerability of indoor building environments to the aerosol transport of pathogens. This article presents the results of numerical modeling of the transport dynamics of virus-containing particles generated during coughing within a room equipped with forced ventilation and domestic air humidification systems. The mathematical model is based on solving the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations for incompressible flow using the standard k–epsilon turbulence model. The Lagrangian approach is applied to describe the trajectories of the discrete phase, accounting for the effects of gravity, aerodynamic drag, Saffman lift forces, and Brownian motion. The SIMPLE numerical algorithm is implemented on a computational mesh exceeding 3.1 million elements. The adequacy of the model is confirmed by verifying the calculated velocity profiles against experimental data and the results of previous studies on cough-driven vortex ring dynamics (Renzi et al.). The study analyzes the influence of ventilation diffusers and the concentration of water vapor from domestic humidifiers on the process of droplet sedimentation and transport. It was established that during an impulsive release of particles at a velocity of 6 m/s, the maximum propagation distance reaches 2.5 m. The results show that active air humidification contributes to a decrease in aerosol concentration and a reduction of the risk zone compared to scenarios without humidity control, where the transport distance exceeds 3.5 m. It is concluded that the standard WHO recommendation for a social distance of two meters may be insufficient without accounting for the operation of indoor climate engineering systems.

title: An integrated framework for multidisciplinary design optimization of unmanned aerial vehicles
authors: Turgunbek Alimov, Jonibek Shukurov, Yusufjon Ergashev, Nuriddin Abdujabarov
abstract: The growing demand for high-performance Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in civil, commercial, and defense applications has increased the need for advanced engineering methodologies capable of addressing complex and often conflicting design requirements. Conventional sequential design approaches generally optimize individual subsystems independently, frequently overlooking the interactions between aerodynamics, structures, propulsion, flight dynamics, control systems, and mission performance. These limitations may result in increased development costs, longer design cycles, and reduced overall system efficiency. This paper proposes an integrated framework for Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO) of UAVs that combines mission analysis, conceptual aircraft design, aerodynamic optimization, structural analysis, propulsion system integration, flight performance evaluation, and system-level optimization within a unified engineering process. The proposed framework facilitates continuous information exchange among engineering disciplines, enabling designers to identify globally optimal solutions while satisfying operational, structural, and aerodynamic constraints. The framework incorporates modern computational tools, including Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Finite Element Analysis (FEA), numerical optimization algorithms, and simulation-based performance evaluation techniques. Furthermore, the study discusses the potential integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms to accelerate design optimization and improve engineering decision-making during the early stages of UAV development. The proposed integrated framework provides a systematic methodology for improving aircraft efficiency, reducing structural weight, minimizing energy consumption, shortening product development time, and enhancing mission effectiveness. The presented approach establishes a foundation for future research on intelligent multidisciplinary optimization of next-generation unmanned aerial systems.

title: Machine learning prediction and analysis of area-averaged external pressure coefficients for low-rise dual-slope building roofs in a uniform turbulent flow field
authors: Mengchang Yang, Yinghang Fu, Yangjin Yuan, Huiling Duan, Jie Wang, Il-seung Yang
abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of roof area-averaged external pressure coefficients ( $${\overline{C}}_{p,A}$$ ) is crucial for low-rise building design. To isolate geometric and turbulence effects from atmospheric wind shear, wind tunnel experiments were conducted under uniform turbulent flow conditions covering roof pitch angles (0°–30°), wind directions, and turbulence intensities. To overcome the smoothing limitations of conventional regression methods, an ensemble learning framework (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) was developed and evaluated using a rigorous Leave-One-Slope-Out (LOSO) cross-validation strategy. Results show that around the roof pitch angle of α = 18.4°, a pronounced variation in aerodynamic pressure response occurs under oblique wind conditions. XGBoost maintains robust predictive performance, outperforming conventional response surface modeling under nonlinear transition conditions. Furthermore, extrapolation failure at α = 30° delineates the practical limits of data-driven models in predicting unseen aerodynamic regimes. Finally, SHAP analysis demonstrates that the model-derived feature attribution patterns are generally consistent with previously reported aerodynamic observations, providing a physically interpretable framework for wind load prediction under complex flow transitions.

title: A comprehensive review of an artificial intelligence-based framework for classifying and solving modified heat partial differential equations
authors: Nabeel Un Nabi, Rao Adeel Un Nabi, Aleeza Hayder, Rashid Ul Haq, Areej Fatima, TieJun Wang, Hassan Abbas Khawaja
abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) fundamentally describe the dynamic relationships among physical quantities and therefore play an essential role in modelling physical processes such as heat transfer, fluid flow, population dynamics, and material behavior, unlike purely algebraic relations. This study presents a critical narrative review of analytical, numerical, and artificial-intelligence-based approaches relevant to modified heat equations, with emphasis on their assumptions, limitations, and suitability for different problem classes. Although some existing hybrid methods integrate governing physics with machine learning to achieve physical informativeness and computational efficiency, such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and neural-operator methods, there remains an unfulfilled need to develop a consistent framework for systematically categorizing modified PDE forms and to identify an appropriate analytical, numerical, and AI-based solution strategy. It provides a critical review of traditional methods of analysis, such as separation of variables, similarity transformations, and perturbation methods, as well as numerical methods, including finite-difference and finite-element methods, alongside modern machine-learning techniques, particularly deep learning networks, and their relative advantages, weaknesses, and integration possibilities. A classification and integration framework of modified heat equations, based on their physical and mathematical properties, is introduced, connecting suitable analytical, numerical, and data-driven solution methods coherently to the complex heat equations. This integrative perspective is intended to support physically interpretable method selection, computational efficiency, and scalable modelling of modified heat equations across scientific and engineering applications.

title: From Design to Bedside: Brain-Targeted Engineered Nanoparticles and Predictive Modeling for Neurodegenerative Diseases Therapeutics
authors: Nguyen Nguyen, Muzhaozi Yuan, Ya Wang
abstract: Nanoparticle (NP)-based drug delivery systems offer promising solutions for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's, which have no cure due to the brain's structural complexity and the restrictive nature of the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Conventional therapeutics, despite strong in vitro efficacy, often fail clinically due to poor brain penetration. Recent advances in NP engineering, including optimization of size (10-100 nm), surface charge (-10 to -20 mV), and targeted ligand decoration, have improved BBB crossing and reduced premature clearance. In parallel, predictive in silico approaches, such as physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, computational fluid dynamics, and machine learning models, enable quantitative prediction of NP biodistribution, residence times, and region-specific uptake. By simulating key determinants, including blood flow dynamics, vasculature heterogeneity, permeability, and retention, these computational tools accelerate lead selection, reduce experimental burden, and inform design before in vivo testing. This review integrates recent progress in NP design with advanced computational modeling, highlighting how their convergence provides a rational framework for developing next-generation brain-targeted therapeutics. We further discuss regulatory and translational challenges, including safety, biocompatibility, and the need for humanized preclinical benchmarks. Together, these innovations offer a roadmap for advancing NP-based strategies toward clinical impact in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Robustness and limitations of fractal-dimension estimation methods for complex fluid interfaces
authors: Marco Herbert, Josef Hasslberger, Maximilian Bambauer, Nilanjan Chakraborty, Markus Klein
abstract: Abstract Fractal geometry provides a useful framework for characterizing highly wrinkled interfaces arising in fluid-dynamical and combustion processes. In this work, the robustness of three methods for estimating the fractal dimension, $$D_f$$ D f , of empirical fractals is assessed: a filtering-based approach, the correlation dimension, and a grid-based box-counting method. The methods are applied to two challenging three-dimensional DNS datasets, namely primary liquid-jet atomization with strong droplet formation and a flame interface subject to Richtmyer-Meshkov instability (RMI). While all three methods show excellent agreement for mathematically defined fractals and reasonable agreement for weakly wrinkled surfaces, they are pushed to their limits for the complex physical interfaces considered here. Differences arise from both numerical sensitivities and the distinct structural and textural features captured by the individual estimators, and may lead to values outside expected or even physical bounds. Although the inferred inner cut-off scales remain within plausible ranges, method-dependent differences persist. For jet atomization, the box-counting method deviates markedly from the other approaches, whereas for the RMI configuration the filtering-based method is the clear outlier. Overall, the results demonstrate that heterogeneous empirical interfaces do not possess a unique, method-independent fractal dimension. Among the investigated methods, the correlation-dimension approach proved to be the most robust and consistently yielded physically plausible estimates across the wide range of interface topologies considered.

title: Vortex dynamic equations for geophysical flows over variable sediment bottoms. Part I: Theoretical framework
authors: Arno Roland Ngatcha Ndengna
abstract: Abstract The present work introduces novel vortex dynamic equations for quasi-geostrophic flows over strongly variable sediment bottoms. The equation considers erosion/deposition exchanges near the bottom and the geometrical changes of the bed interface, extending some of the most commonly used vortex dynamic equations in the literature. The derivation of these equations is presented in great detail, including all physical and hydrodynamic mechanisms involved. A novel potential vorticity theorem is presented, elucidating the essential role of sediment exchange and bottom movement in the generation and destruction of vorticity. The presented equations illustrate that several mechanisms, including sediment exchanges and movement of the bed interface, are responsible for vortex dynamics (generation and destruction of the vortex). The paper also presents various related vortex dynamic equations, which are of particular interest for coastal engineering applications. The consolidation of the nonhomogeneous Navier-Stokes equations, in conjunction with sediment transport, into a single equation is proven to be feasible. The merits of our modeling approach are elucidated, and several observations are made.

title: Machine Learning Surrogate Modelling of Aerodynamic Efficiency (Cl/Cd)
authors: Arif Ali Rind, M. R. Luhur, Muhammad Kashif Abbasi, A. Abbasi, S. Bhangwar
abstract: High-fidelity aerodynamic evaluation of airfoils is computationally expensive for multidimensional design and operating-condition studies. This study develops a comparative and explainable machine-learning surrogate framework to predict the aerodynamic efficiency lift to drag ratio (CL/CD) of the SG6043 airfoil family and its modified variants. A dataset of 924 observations covering 26 airfoil configurations was developed over Reynolds numbers of (1.0× 105 – 6.0× 105 ), angles of attack of 2.5–10°, thickness ratios of 5.00 – 10.02%, and camber ratios of 5.00 – 9.00%. Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were evaluated using an 80:20 train– test split. The ANN, comprising two hidden layers of 100 and 50 neurons, achieved the best performance with (R2 =0.9967), RMSE = 2.246, MAE = 1.457, and MAPE = 1.68%, compared with (R2 =0.8462) and MAPE = 12.61% for MLR. RF and XGBoost achieved (R2=0.9929) and 0.9946, respectively. SHAP analysis identified Reynolds number as the dominant predictor, followed by camber, angle of attack, and thickness. The ANN exhibited negligible prediction bias (0.179) and 94.59% empirical coverage for the nominal 95% prediction interval. The results demonstrate that ANN-based surrogate modelling can accurately capture the nonlinear (CL/CD) response within the investigated SG6043 design space, providing an efficient and interpretable approach for rapid airfoil screening, sensitivity analysis, and aerodynamic optimization.

title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Methods for Laser-Based Diagnostics: From Measurement Physics to Autonomous Sensing Systems
authors: Saleh Mahmoud, Turki AlQemlas
abstract: Laser-based diagnostic techniques are indispensable for non-intrusive, high-resolution measurements in fluid mechanics, combustion, and multiphase flows. However, modern experiments increasingly generate high-dimensional spatiotemporal datasets that strain traditional workflows and remain limited by core measurement-physics constraints, including signal-to-noise degradation, spatiotemporal resolution trade-offs, calibration uncertainty, and real-time processing demands. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) offer new capabilities for automated feature extraction, physics-aware reconstruction, Uncertainty Quantification (UQ), and real-time inference. This review synthesizes AI-enabled advances across laser velocimetry, fluorescence thermometry and species imaging, soot diagnostics, and tomographic/volumetric reconstruction. The review covers supervised and self-supervised deep learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Bayesian uncertainty-aware approaches, and generative models, emphasizing how these methods address measurement-physics limitations and what is required for reliable experimental deployment. A comparative synthesis highlights cross-modality trade-offs in accuracy, interpretability, scalability, and real-time capability, and identifies persistent challenges including generalization to unseen conditions, physical consistency, calibrated uncertainty, and closed-loop integration. The review concludes with a forward-looking framework and roadmap toward physics-aware, uncertainty-informed autonomous laser diagnostics capable of adaptive measurement strategies and real-time decision-making in complex experimental environments.

title: A Computational Framework for Groundwater Flow and Solute Migration in Layered Aquifers
authors: Sherzod Daliev, Mashxura Kushanova, Zulaykho Nazarova, Muhammadi Turayev, Oxun Xaitov, Sobir Igamov, Elyor Shavkiev
abstract: Understanding the coupled dynamics of groundwater flow and salinity transport is crucial for the sustainable management of aquifer systems, particularly in irrigated and semi-arid regions where evaporation, recharge variability, and groundwater abstraction significantly alter hydrogeological regimes. In multilayer porous media, groundwater-level fluctuations and salt migration are strongly interdependent, as hydraulic gradients govern solute transport and salinity variations may influence flow behavior through density-dependent mechanisms. This study develops a nonlinear mathematical model for describing groundwater-level evolution and salinity transport in a two-layer porous medium composed of an upper phreatic aquifer and an underlying confined aquifer. The model incorporates filtration processes, interlayer hydraulic exchange, density-dependent effects, and external forcing factors, including surface recharge, evaporation, and pumping. For numerical implementation, the governing equations are discretized using a finite-difference scheme with central spatial approximations and an implicit Crank–Nicolson-type temporal formulation. A hybrid second-order time approximation is introduced for the phreatic-layer equation to enhance numerical smoothness, stability, and convergence behavior. The resulting tridiagonal algebraic systems are solved by the Thomas algorithm within an iterative quasi-linearization framework, ensuring computational efficiency and robustness for nonlinear coupled simulations. The simulation results demonstrate distinct dynamic responses in the two aquifer layers. The phreatic aquifer responds rapidly and with higher amplitude to external forcing, whereas the confined aquifer exhibits slower, smoother, and more inertial hydraulic and geochemical adjustments. Sensitivity analysis shows that the filtration coefficient, transmissivity, porosity, density-dependent parameters, surface fluxes, and pumping intensity are the key factors controlling groundwater-level variations and salinity redistribution. The proposed modeling framework provides a reliable computational tool for analyzing coupled groundwater–salinity processes and offers a scientifically grounded basis for groundwater monitoring, salinization risk assessment, and sustainable aquifer management in multilayer hydrogeological systems.

title: AI-based multilayer soft computing analysis for convective heating in 3D Eyring-Powell nanofluids flow on stretching sheet
authors: Deli Lin, Abdinn Albadri, Zahoor Shah, Hamza Iqbal, Amina magdich, Hafedh Mahmoud Zayani
abstract: :- Employing state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks fundamentally enhances the analytical capabilities within fluid dynamics, facilitating the sophisticated modeling and resolution of complex, non-linear systems with an unprecedented degree of precision and computational sophistication. This paper concerned with an in-depth analysis of three-dimensional flow of Eyring-Powell nanofluid over an exponentially stretching sheet with convective heating conditions (3D-EPNFM) by application of AI-based multilayer intelligent computing associated with Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm (MLIC-LMA). The basic mathematical expression of 3D-EPNFM was initially reduced into a set of nonlinear dimension-less ODEs, along with their boundary conditions by utilizing a non-dimensionalities technique. We constructed a reference dataset for the model by systematically altering various parameters across multiple scenarios while keeping some of the parameters fixed. This dataset was further employed to the training, validation, and testing processes of the proposed MLIC-LMA framework. The outcomes of MLIC-LMA consistently correspond with numerical findings across all variations of presented model, exhibiting minimal errors which is negligible. The analysis reveals outstanding performance in term of mean square error (MSE) across all situations, with values recorded as E-08, E-09, E-07, E-09, E-08, E-11, E-09, E-08, E-10, and E-12, corresponding to 287, 349, 162, 286, 329, 722, 913, 854, 347, and 345 final epochs, respectively. The accuracy of proposed MLIC-LMA is validated through its performance using various metrics, including performance curve graphs, error histograms, MSE, and regression analysis.

title: Local Consistency Does Not Guarantee Global Conservation: Auditing Zero-Shot Composition of Airway Flow Operators
authors: Nichula Sathmith Wasalathilaka, Navodya Heshan Samarasinghe Dhanujaya Suraweera, Kevin Dawson, Chinthaka Jacob Mervyn Parakrama Bandara Ekanayake, Roshan Godaliyadda
abstract: Neural operators approximate PDE solutions within a geometry family, but independently learned local operators need not form a consistent global simulator. We study frozen, single-pass composition for steady incompressible flow in idealized two-dimensional airway trees. Separate Tube, bifurcation, and trifurcation DeepONets are trained on 4,872 primitive CFD cases using field supervision and auxiliary divergence, port-flux, component-balance, and port-pressure penalties. The validation-selected deployment is frozen before whole-tree CFD fields are inspected and assembled without tree training, iterative coupling, flux correction, or CFD-informed adjustment. It retains major flow patterns and controlled pathology responses with 0.204-0.215 s CPU inference, but has a 22.68% prescribed-inlet-normalized external residual. A post-hoc sensitivity protocol, frozen before new training and evaluation, repeats Data, Div, and Full models across three seeds with Tube fixed. Relative to Data, Full reduces primitive composite scores by 26.7% for Y2 and 26.4% for Y3 and reduces assembled component-residual and interface-mismatch RMS by 7.2% and 16.6%, respectively. Nevertheless, mean tree velocity error increases by 7.5%, while external residual increases from 17.49 +/- 4.38% to 26.77 +/- 3.65%. Local regularization can therefore improve primitive and assembled local diagnostics without ensuring accurate global fields or conservation.

title: Meter-scale pedestrian PET and cooling-lever attribution with an ai surrogate: a microclimate digital twin for a heat-resilient Barcelona superblock
authors: Sohei Yamada, Severin Brochhagen, Camilo E. Rojas-Sanchez, Jorge Garcia Vidal, Hossein Arefi, Masoud Ghandehari, Mariano Lamarca-Llorente
abstract: Pedestrian heat stress, expressed as physiologically equivalent temperature (PET), swings across dangerous thresholds within meters as sun, tree shade, and building shadow change, yet weather and satellite data are too coarse to resolve it, and city heat indicators do not map to what a pedestrian feels. For a superblock in Barcelona, we compute meter-scale diurnal pedestrian PET from measurement-driven unsteady CFD (with and without vegetation) and shade-aware radiation post-processing, and validate its air, humidity, and surface-temperature inputs against mobile transects, contact points, and a thermal camera. We decompose street-tree cooling into shade, evapotranspiration, and wind, compare heat measures on one PET metric, and train a machine-learning surrogate that rebuilds the block field in seconds. On a clear July afternoon, after correcting a validated warm-air bias, most of the block reaches strong heat stress; tree cooling is almost entirely shade and concentrates where the canopy shadow falls, while reflective pavement raises pedestrian PET even as it cools the road. The surrogate reproduces the sun/shade field at a thousandth of the cost, a same-day validated microclimate digital twin that maps pedestrian heat at street and hour scale and weighs the city's canopy target, reflective-pavement pilot, and shelter network on one measure.

title: Impact of Surface Geometry on Vortex Dynamics in Fluid Flows of Different Velocities
authors: Nika Poorshahrezaei
abstract: This paper will investigate the subject of fluid behavior upon interaction with various geometries.Observations about the different shapes of airplane wings depending on the purpose of the plane caused questioning about the functionality of the wingshape in particular aerial conditions.These questions were further elaborated on and understood by constructing a model wind tunnel used to test numerous variations of objects to determine how air flow is affected by different characteristics of an aerial body, such as the wingtip of an airfoil creating vortices and what implications that may have on the fluid overall, similar to the intent of different cylindrical bodies and how the bluntness of their shape impacts the fluid.A multitude of tests at three different speeds, analyzed by the intensity and frequency of vortices, revealed that airfoils maintain stability with attached flow, while cylindrical and wavy shapes exhibit high drag, early separation, and, in the case of concave surfaces, extreme instability.Surface roughness acts as a velocity-dependent turbulator, reducing displacement at low speeds but catalyzing premature vortex shedding at higher velocities.These results have major implications for aerial and nautical travel in terms of efficiency, safety, and the extent of human travel.

title: A semi analytical simulation and Bayesian Regularization technique for thermophoretic particle deposition in radiative nanofluid flow with Brownian motion and Stefan blowing impacts
authors: Muhammad Azhar Iqbal, M. Saif Aldien, Abaker A. Hassaballa, Asma A. Alhashmi, Ansar Abbas, Gulnar Hamidova Abdulhamid
abstract: By using the computational power of Bayesian Regularization Optimizer Supervised Neural Networks (BRO-SNNs), this semi-analytical model, which investigates thermophoretic particle deposition in a Boger nanofluid flow over an inclined sheet using Brownian motion and Stefan blowing, has important applications in advanced heat management and materials processing. It provides a key framework for enhancing heat exchanger designs, demonstrating how controlled nanoparticle deposition can improve heat transfer or avoid surface fouling. The findings are immediately applicable to coating and thin-film manufacturing processes, allowing for fine control over deposit uniformity and thickness by manipulating thermophoresis and Stefan blowing. Furthermore, the model can be used in environmental engineering to estimate particle deposition in scrubbers and filtration systems, as well as in aircraft to manage dust or ice formation on critical components. The viscoelastic character of Boger fluids makes it especially useful for creating next-generation smart cooling systems based on polymer-based nanofluids. The HAM solves the non-dimensional non-linear governing ODEs (ordinary differential equations) that are derived following appropriate similarity transformations. The velocity field upsurges as increase the values of nanoparticles solvent friction while thermal profile decline.

title: Multiphase transport interactions across multilayer proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers
authors: P. C. Sidharth, Alberto Antonini, Yousef Heider, Giovanna Xotta, Valentina Anna Lia Salomoni, B.N. Rao, Fadi Aldakheel
abstract: The performance of Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers (PEMWE) at high current densities is governed by a complex interplay between mechanical assembly, electrochemical kinetics, and hydraulic transport. To quantify the impact of mechanical compression on Ohmic resistance and species transport, this study employs a thermodynamically consistent framework based on the Theory of Porous Media (TPM), implemented in FEniCSx (open-access finite element package) via a calibrated conductivity scaling approach. We demonstrate that mechanical clamping forces induce significant heterogeneity in the porosity, where localized densification under the Porous Transport Layer (PTL) lands creates structural and capillary bottlenecks that fundamentally alter the displacement of liquid water by evolved gases. Our results reveal that electrochemical activity is highly localized at the membrane interfaces, where gas accumulation triggers sharp hydraulic pressure gradients necessary to force products through the deformed pore network. High compression enhances electrical connectivity but exacerbates liquid depletion. Regions beneath the flow channels, by contrast, retain comparatively higher liquid saturation than the compressed land regions, acting as preferential transport corridors even at high current densities. While the absolute saturation level is influenced by the prescribed channel boundary condition, the land–channel contrast itself, and its increase with compression ratio, is an emergent consequence of compression-induced porosity and permeability heterogeneity. These findings extend PEMWE optimization beyond the conventional focus on contact resistance by showing that the balance between ionic conductivity and mass transport is governed by the mechanical architecture of the assembly. The proposed framework further enables predictive mechanical–hydraulic co-design of next-generation high-power electrolyzer architectures. The corresponding source codes are openly available at https://doi.org/10.25835/nll5g6i6 to ensure reproducibility and facilitate further research by the scientific community.

title: Materials and architected structures for underbody blast mitigation in armoured fighting vehicles: From conventional protection systems to additively manufactured metallic lattices
authors: Ameer Malik Shaik, B. Veera Siva Reddy, D. Akhil Kumar, A. Hafeezur Rahman, C. Chandrasekhara Sastry, Robert Cep
abstract: Armoured Fighting Vehicles (AFVs) must survive distinct but interacting threat classes, including kinetic-energy and armour-piercing projectiles, shaped-charge jets, high-velocity fragments, top-attack munitions, and buried mine/IED blast. This review therefore positions underbody energy absorbers within the wider layered protection architecture, while deliberately focusing its detailed assessment on mine/IED blast mitigation. Conventional metallic armour, ceramic-backed and fibre-reinforced systems, reactive protection, active protection, V-shaped hulls, metallic foams, aluminium honeycombs, and additively manufactured lattices are compared according to their primary protection function and appropriate performance metrics. Particular attention is given to laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of A286 alloy because it combines precipitation-strengthened mechanical properties, corrosion and thermal stability, and practical LPBF processability with emerging high-strain-rate evidence. A286 is not treated as a ballistic replacement for RHA, MHA, HHA, or HNS; rather, A286 lattices are evaluated as sacrificial energy-absorbing elements intended to operate together with a structural hull and primary ballistic protection. The review separates quasi-static screening, Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) characterization, impact testing, and explosive-blast validation, and links LPBF porosity, lack-of-fusion defects, surface roughness, residual stress, and anisotropy to dynamic collapse and failure. The applicability of the Maxwell criterion is restricted to pin-jointed strut networks, whereas TPMS behaviour is discussed using surface/shell mechanics, curvature, relative density, and observed deformation modes. Ashby-type normalized maps and recent AI-enabled approaches are incorporated to compare architected systems and support defect detection, topology optimization, high-rate response prediction, and digital-twin design. The resulting framework identifies the evidence still required to translate LPBF lattices from coupon-scale energy absorbers to qualified, modular underbody blast-mitigation components in integrated AFV protection systems.

title: A condition-driven globally aware point cloud network for rapid surface field prediction of cross-domain flight vehicles
authors: Shi-Zhe Yu, Ming-Yao Lin, Sheng-Bao Wu, Xin Li, Gang Chen
abstract: Rapid prediction of aerodynamic and aerothermal surface fields is critical for the design and real-time monitoring of cross-domain flight vehicles, yet conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) remains prohibitively expensive. Here, a condition-driven globally aware point cloud network (CD-GPN) is presented, achieving millisecond-scale, near-CFD-accuracy predictions of surface pressure and heat flux. Based on PointNeXt, CD-GPN integrates three core components: geometrically enhanced inverted residual modules for local geometric perception; a condition feature modulation mechanism via feature-wise linear modulation to inject flight conditions into deep feature streams; and a global interaction module on condition-modulated latent modes to capture long-range flow-field correlations. Extensively tested across Mach 5–15, altitudes of 20–40 km, and angles of attack of 0°–10°, CD-GPN outperforms mainstream baselines. Specifically, it yields a mean normalized root mean square error of 1.77% for single-configuration pressure prediction, and 1.03% and 2.07% for multi-configuration pressure and heat flux predictions, respectively. Furthermore, it demonstrates good extrapolation robustness to unseen flight conditions and novel geometries, and transfer fine-tuning with only a small number of target-configuration samples can further reduce the cross-topology blind-prediction error. Meanwhile, in terms of efficiency, it reduces the single evaluation time from 45 min (CFD) to 134 ms. These results establish CD-GPN as an efficient, physics-aware surrogate bridging offline simulation and online monitoring for next-generation aerospace vehicle design.

title: Machine-Learning Surrogates for Airfoil Pitching Moment: Accuracy, Extrapolation, and the Finite-Thickness Shift of the Aerodynamic Center
authors: Ishaan Srichitturi
abstract: Abstract The pitching-moment coeﬀicient of an airfoil, together with lift and drag, is needed for stability and trim calculations, and machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to replace repeated physics-based solver runs. This paper studies such a surrogate in a testbed where the physics is known exactly: the quarter-chord pitching-moment coeﬀicient Cm of NACA 4-digit airfoils, computed from a potential-flow panel method. The panel method’s moment output is checked against thin-airfoil theory at five cambered sections (agreement within 3%) and against the exact zero-moment result for a symmetric section (2 × 10−17, machine precision). A secondary, quantified finding emerges from this check: the finite-thickness panel method’s aerodynamic center is not exactly at the quarter-chord predicted by thin-airfoil theory, but shifts aft by 0.008–0.016 chord as thickness increases from 6% to 18%, almost independent of camber; evaluating Cm at this fitted center instead of a fixed quarter-chord collapses its variation with angle of attack by more than an order of magnitude (by a factor of 20 to 80, depending on section). A random forest and a linear-regression baseline are then compared on 1,674 computed cases under repeated random splits, permutation feature importance, and 48 queries outside the training ranges. Inside the training range the forest reaches a mean held-out R2 of 0.999, and the inputs it relies on match the physics: importance is concentrated in the two camber inputs, with angle of attack and thickness contributing little, consistent with Cm being governed by camber shape and only weakly by angle of attack. Outside the training range, the forest’s accuracy is affected much less by new angles of attack (R2 = 0.95) than by new airfoil shapes (R2 = 0.73), and the spread of predictions across its trees does not distinguish the two cases (it changes by under 1% while the mean error increases by a factor of 19), so it still gives no warning. Because the target quantity is nearly flat over part of its input space, this testbed also shows that a tree ensemble’s extrapolation failure mode, returning a roughly constant value, can be far less costly when the true function happens to be close to that constant.

title: Development of a Quasi-Static MHD Solver for Turbulent Flows with Non-Uniform Applied Magnetic Fields in OpenFOAM
authors: Wellington Fonseca
abstract: Abstract The magnetic-induction implementation of low-magnetic-Reynolds-number (low-Rm ) magnetohydrodynamics develops a severe discrete cancellation error when the applied magnetic field is not uniform. The Lorentz force is evaluated in Maxwell-stress form as the difference of two terms of order B02 /(µ0ρL), an acceleration in m.s−2 — the force per unit volume divided by ρ; that cancellation is exact at the continuous level, but its discrete counterpart is exact only for a uniform imposed field. A non-uniform field therefore leaves a residual body force that grows with the square of the applied field and, as Sect. 5.6 shows, does not decrease over the refinement range investigated. For a 10 T field in a 0.15 m duct it reaches 103 m.s−2 , two orders of magnitude above the physical Lorentz acceleration, and the solution diverges within two time steps. Then, was developed the mhdturbFoamQS (QS for quasi-static), a finite-volume OpenFOAM solver that removes the residual by construction. The current density is obtained from the electric-potential (quasi-static) formulation and the Lorentz force is evaluated directly as j×B0 , so that no quantity of order B02 /(µ0ρL) is ever subtracted from another. The applied field is prescribed as a general volVectorField rather than a constant; the insulating-wall condition j · n = 0 is imposed consistently on both sides of the discrete potential equation; and the stiff magnetic sink is discretised implicitly, so that magnetic damping no longer restricts the time step. The standard OpenFOAM closures are used unmodified, which isolates the electromagnetic formulation from additional turbulence-model changes. Verification against the exact Hartmann solution reproduces the friction factor within 0.17 % and the velocity profile within 0.5 %, and the solver is further assessed against the Shercliff–Gold solution for a circular pipe with insulating walls. The solver and its verification case are released under GPL v3 with a concept DOI on Zenodo.

title: Early-Time Filtrate Invasion Modeling During Primary Drilling-In of Terrigenous Oil Reservoirs
authors: В. И. Никитин, George V. Buslaev, Mikhail E. Lamosov, T. A. Panteleeva
abstract: Accurate interpretation of geological and technological data acquired during drilling largely depends on understanding the interaction between drilling fluid and the productive formation at the initial stage of reservoir penetration. One of the least investigated phenomena affecting the reliability of well logging and gas logging interpretation is ahead-of-bit filtration, in which drilling fluid filtrate invades the formation before its physical exposure by the drill bit. This study aims to develop the scientific basis for a methodology to calculate the parameters of the formation fluid displacement front caused by ahead-of-bit filtration during the primary penetration of terrigenous oil-bearing reservoirs. The proposed methodology combines an analytical description of drilling fluid spurt loss with a two-phase flow model to predict filtrate invasion under downhole conditions. An algorithm was developed to calculate the principal parameters governing the displacement process along the wellbore axis, including filtrate invasion volume, filtrate saturation, penetration depth, and the position of the formation fluid displacement front. The analytical formulation enables laboratory and bench-scale filtration data to be extrapolated to actual drilling conditions, thereby improving the prediction of filtrate invasion during reservoir penetration. The developed approach provides a quantitative framework for evaluating the influence of ahead-of-bit filtration on reservoir fluid saturation and the interpretation of gas logging measurements obtained from drilled cuttings. Application of the proposed methodology demonstrated that the presence of drilling fluid filtrate leads to an underestimation of the native fluid saturation, with the filtrate fraction reaching 4.35% in the investigated case. The proposed methodology offers an effective tool for improving the interpretation accuracy of geological and technological drilling data and supports more reliable characterization of productive formations during the primary penetration stage.

title: Uncertainty in Precipitation Estimates Warrants Greater Consideration in Debris‐Flow Research
authors: Ann E Sinclair, Nina S. Oakley, A. Joshua West, Marin Kristen Clark, Daniel E. Horton
abstract: Abstract Quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) may provide a valuable data resource for investigations of postfire debris flows. In mountainous regions where debris flows typically occur, gauge coverage can be sparse; gridded QPEs offer remotely sensed and/or physics‐based precipitation estimates where no direct measurement is available. However, different gridded QPEs often tell contrasting stories about the magnitude, timing, and location of precipitation during a storm, which can lead to biases or misrepresentations of triggering rainfall in debris‐flow studies. Here, we explore the utility of different gridded QPEs for capturing debris‐flow triggering intensities at hazard relevant scales (∼1–10 km, hourly). We present a comparison of 12 QPE products at the time and location of postfire debris‐flow occurrence during seven recent storms in southern California. At all debris‐flow locations, we found substantial differences in the timing and intensities reported by QPE products. Across all events, peak storm intensities from gridded QPEs ranged from 100% lower than gauge observations to over 600% higher. In assessing QPE differences in the context of gauge‐based operational triggering thresholds, we found that threshold exceedance varies with the choice of QPE. Our results suggest that QPE product differences limit our current ability to constrain debris‐flow triggering precipitation. We provide recommendations to account for QPE differences and to more effectively and transparently use gridded QPEs in debris‐flow applications.

title: Learning cylinder wake dynamics across Hopf bifurcation via a regime-adaptive dual-branch physics-informed neural network
authors: Cong Li, Q Wang, Wei Song
abstract: The ability to represent fluid dynamics across regime transitions remains a fundamental challenge in physics-informed machine learning. In cylinder wake flows, the Hopf bifurcation at the critical Reynolds number Rec≈52 induces a transition from a steady, nearly symmetric base state to periodic von Kármán vortex shedding, accompanied by a qualitative reorganization of the underlying solution manifold. This raises a key question of whether nonlinear fluid systems admit a unified neural representation across bifurcation-induced reorganization of the solution manifold. Here, we propose a regime-adaptive dual-branch physics-informed neural network to investigate this question. The model explicitly decomposes the solution space into steady and unsteady dynamical components, which are coupled through a continuous Re-dependent gating mechanism centered at Rec≈52, thereby reducing cross-regime interference during optimization. To ensure stable learning under continuous parameterization, we combine continuous Reynolds-number feature embeddings with a multi-stage curriculum learning protocol that progressively restores the contributions of time-resolved observations and transient physical constraints while retaining the complete Reynolds-number range throughout training. Using supervised computational fluid dynamics data at 11 Reynolds numbers over 5≤Re≤120, the framework is evaluated on six held-out in-range Reynolds numbers and two extrapolation cases, Re=2 and 126. The model accurately reconstructs the principal wake structures and key flow statistics at unseen Reynolds numbers, with particularly strong performance across the held-out in-range cases. These results show that explicitly encoding regime separation in the neural architecture improves the representation of bifurcation-induced solution-manifold reorganization and enables continuous parametric surrogate modeling across steady and periodically shedding wake regimes.

title: A physics-oriented review of neural-network-based modeling for bluff-body flows
authors: Xin Tang, Jingnan Zhang, Heng Zhu
abstract: Bluff-body flows combine early separation, coherent wake organization, vortex shedding, and strong sensitivity to geometry, Reynolds number, inflow condition, and three-dimensional transition. These features make them both canonical fluid-mechanics benchmarks and demanding targets for neural-network-based modeling. This review provides a representative, physics-oriented synthesis of neural-network approaches for bluff-body flows. Instead of organizing the field by architecture or prediction task, the review asks which wake mechanisms current models represent and which validation evidence makes those claims trustworthy. It examines how current models represent separation, wake topology, pressure-wake coupling, coherent shedding, turbulence statistics, closure behavior, and flow-control mechanisms. We discuss data sources, flow representations, model classes, validation practices, and practical uses in surrogate prediction, reconstruction, monitoring, control, and digital-twin-type workflows. The review emphasizes that low numerical error by itself does not establish physical learning, and argues for validation based on topology, spectra, force response, uncertainty, generalization, and interpretable mechanism evidence.

title: Baseline-informed Fourier neural operator correction for nonlinear wave loads on monopile foundations under steep regular waves
authors: Jianxiang Yi, Yulin Xie, Baoli Deng, Changbo Jiang
abstract: Reliable prediction of horizontal wave loads remains important for preliminary assessment of offshore monopile foundations under steep regular waves. The Rainey semi-analytical model efficiently predicts the dominant periodic load but does not fully capture local waveform features associated with secondary load cycles. This study uses computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations as the numerical reference and defines the difference from the Rainey solution as a correction target over one wave period. A Fourier neural operator (FNO) learns this correction from dimensionless wave and geometry parameters and the complete Rainey force history; adding the predicted correction to the Rainey baseline yields the Theory+FNO total force. On 20 independent test cases, Theory+FNO and Rainey give mean total-force normalized root mean square errors of 2.56% and 9.08%, respectively, against the CFD reference. The correction improves the representation of local secondary load-cycle features and gives lower errors than direct total-force FNO prediction in the complete diameter holdouts. The framework provides rapid horizontal-load estimates for circular monopiles within the investigated range of steep regular waves.

title: From fiber formation to function: A comprehensive review of microfluidic spinning for biomedical and technological applications
authors: Helena P. Felgueiras
abstract: Microfluidic spinning has matured from a niche fabrication method into a general-purpose platform for engineering fibers to specification, where diameter, cross-sectional architecture, mechanical anisotropy, and surface chemistry become deliberately tunable design parameters, albeit ones that remain mechanistically coupled to one another through the shared flow conditions that set them, rather than incidental byproducts of the spinning process. This review traces that platform end to end: the fluid dynamics and solidification chemistries that govern fiber formation in a microchannel; the natural, synthetic, and composite materials systems available for spinning; the device architectures, from glass capillaries to three-dimensional printed spinnerets, that translate those materials into continuous fibers; and the structural and functional design strategies, core-shell and Janus architectures, aligned and porous morphologies, stimuli-responsive compartments, that turn a simple filament into a programmable one. The review then surveys how this design space has been applied, spanning tissue engineering scaffolds, drug delivery systems, cell encapsulation and bioprinting, and organ-on-a-fiber devices in the biomedical space, and extending into wearable electronics, energy storage, and photonic fibers beyond it. Recurring engineering bottlenecks, the trade-off between throughput and precision, materials incompatibility across core-sheath pairings, and the field's lack of standardized reporting metrics, are examined critically, alongside the still largely unrealized potential for closed-loop, sensor-guided process control to address them. It is concluded that microfluidic spinning's next phase will depend less on new spinning chemistries than on hybridization with electrospinning and additive manufacturing, and on closer collaboration between microfluidics, materials science, and bioengineering to translate designer fibers from laboratory demonstrations into reproducible, application-ready platforms.

title: CFD Investigation of Thermal and Electrical Behavior of Photovoltaic Modules Equipped with Heat Sinks and Vortex Generators
authors: A. J. Al-Maliki, Davood Domiri Ganji, Mofid Gorji-Bandpy
abstract: The Photovoltaic (PV) modules suffer performance losses at high operating temperatures, especially in hot and low-wind conditions, making effective cooling essential. This study numerically investigates a fan-assisted PV cooling duct equipped with heat sinks and vortex generators (VGs) using computational fluid dynamics (CFD). The novelty of the work lies in the integrated evaluation of duct height, fin spacing, VG height, inclination angle, and attack angle within a single forced-convection framework. The model was validated against published benchmark data with deviations below 5%. The results demonstrate that the reduction of duct height from 200 mm to 100 mm can decrease the PV surface temperature by 10 °C and among all finned cases, the array with 22 fins exhibited maximum cooling whilst the best compromise between heat-transfer enhancement and pressure drop was provided by using an arrangement with 18 fins in a given area. Thermal performance improved with increasing VG height, but the 40 mm VG gave the greatest heat-transfer coefficient at the cost of relatively high-pressure loss. In the 90° case, VG orientation achieved the highest electrical efficiency at (Re = 11000), achieving an electrical efficiency of 16.9% and maximum achievable electrical power output of approximately 44.21 W, after accounting for DC fan power consumption, with the 90° VG configuration still showing the highest system electrical power. The 30° scenario, by contrast, resulted in the best thermal efficiency–nearly 80% and the greatest thermal power–over 420 W demonstrating practical merit in providing guidance for selecting PV cooling configurations based on specific electrical-output or thermal-recovery priorities.

title: Numerical and multi-objective optimal design of bionic corrugated plate-fins heat exchangers by extreme learning machine algorithm
authors: Chao Yu, Guangyi Wang, Xiangyao Xue, Mengyang Wang, Jiarun Lou, Zelin Wang
abstract: Abstract The structural characteristics of the fins determine the performance of heat exchanger. An outstanding fin structure exhibits high heat transfer performance and low flow resistance, which are conflicting outcomes. Through natural evolution, fish have developed a shape structure suitable for swimming. Inspired by this, this research presents a biomimetic corrugated fin structure based on the fins of eels. The extreme learning machine algorithm is used to construct a surrogate model. The NSGA-III multi-objective optimization method is chosen to optimize the corrugated fin heat exchanger. In comparison with the traditional corrugated fin, the optimized biomimetic fin shows 4.7% enhancement in heat transfer performance and 6.1% decrease in the resistance coefficient. Based on the simulation results, the characteristics of the internal flow field of the fin are analyzed from the perspectives of velocity, temperature, and pressure. This study also incorporates the field synergy theory. By constructing the field synergy equation to calculate the synergy angle between velocity and temperature, the performance advantages of the biomimetic fin are further verified. The proposed novel fin can offer a new alternative for high-performance heat exchangers, and the simulation optimization method can provide a new approach for engineers to design heat exchanger fins.

title:
Improving wind flow simulation over complex terrain for wind resource assessment through a hybrid data-driven and physics-informed generalized k–
 
 ω
 
 framework
authors: Guo-Lin Ma, Lin-Lin Tian, Yi-Lei Song, Ning Zhao
abstract: Accurate prediction of wind speed and turbulence over complex terrain remains challenging because terrain-induced separation and atmospheric boundary layer turbulence are not fully represented by conventional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) closure models. This study develops Mod-GEKO-ML, a hybrid framework combining adjoint optimization and machine learning (ML) calibration of spatially varying generalized k–ω (GEKO) free coefficients with physics-informed modification of selected traditional closure constants. The GEKO-ML mapping is trained on the H42 bump, tested on H38 and H31 for in-family transfer, and applied without retraining to Askervein Hill and Bolund Island. The turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) objective best balances mean flow and turbulence improvement, while reducing the input from eight features to five preserves predictive capability. Field scale evaluations demonstrate partial- and region-dependent transferability, with improved wind speed prediction in terrain affected regions and consistent TKE error reduction. Component analysis shows that ML calibration mainly improves local terrain-induced mean flow responses, whereas closure modification improves upstream TKE preservation and contributes more strongly to TKE error reduction. Feature space analysis shows that H42 training support varies across terrain regions and does not directly determine ML improvement. At Askervein Hill, Mod-GEKO-ML reduces lee side root mean square error (RMSE) by 13.7% for wind speed and 44.8% for TKE relative to standard GEKO. At Bolund Island, TKE RMSE decreases in all three terrain regions under both inflow directions. This framework provides a practical RANS-based approach for wind flow and turbulence prediction over complex terrain.

title: Time–frequency mode decomposition for wind turbine vibration monitoring under variable speed operation
authors: Wei Zhou, Weijian Li, Desen Zhu, Hongbin Xu, Wei-Xin Ren
abstract: Wind turbine vibration monitoring under variable speed operation requires separating nonstationary rotor-order components whose frequencies and operating intervals depend on operating state. These components can occupy local support regions in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) plane rather than fixed spectral bands or continuous ridges. This study presents time–frequency mode decomposition (TFMD), which defines each mode as the time domain signal reconstructed by inverse STFT from one connected support region in the STFT plane. Signal decomposition thereby becomes the estimation of an unknown number of connected support regions. In a synthetic response with six operating states, TFMD separates the component active in each state and produces low reconstruction error without specifying the number of components in advance. In a controlled wind turbine blade strain experiment, the first decomposition reconstructs nine modes whose peak frequencies lie near the nominal once per revolution frequencies and whose energies are concentrated in the corresponding operating intervals. Residual decomposition further reveals the weaker twice per revolution harmonics of all nine operating states. These results support TFMD as a practical candidate for vibration analysis under variable speed operation, while offshore field use requires validation under environmental loading and with measured operating references.

title: Spacing Effects in Guided Vertical‐Axis Wind Turbine Arrays for Highway Energy Harvesting Under Multi‐Vehicle Wake Conditions
authors: Aydin Ulus, Stefan Ilie Moldovan
abstract: ABSTRACT Highway‐induced airflow generated by passing vehicles represents an underutilized source of localized renewable energy that can be harvested using vertical‐axis wind turbines (VAWTs). While prior studies have demonstrated the feasibility of single‐turbine configurations, the aerodynamic interaction between vehicle wakes and multi‐turbine arrays—particularly the role of inter‐turbine spacing—remains insufficiently understood. In this study, two‐dimensional unsteady Reynolds‐averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) simulations coupled with the SST k–ω turbulence model are employed to investigate the performance of guided elliptical Savonius‐type VAWT arrays operating under multi‐vehicle traffic conditions. Three‐turbine arrays are examined at normalized inter‐turbine spacings from S/D = 3 to 14, together with an additional phase‐aligned reference case at S/D = 30.114. The results reveal a strong non‐linear dependence of array‐level energy extraction on turbine spacing. Among the investigated configurations, the highest total energy capture is achieved at a spacing of 12 m (12D), yielding a total extracted energy of 697.34 J and representing a 68% increase relative to the most compact configuration. Smaller spacings are characterized by severe wake interference between turbines, whereas larger spacings exhibit progressive dissipation of vehicle‐induced flow structures despite near‐complete velocity recovery. Turbine 1 shows limited sensitivity to spacing, with an energy variation of approximately 14%, whereas Turbines 2 and 3 exhibit substantially greater variations of approximately 87% and more than 140%, respectively. The inclusion of guide vanes further enhances total energy extraction by approximately 80–120% across the investigated spacing range. These findings highlight the importance of coordinated inter‐turbine spacing and flow‐guiding strategies in maximizing energy harvesting from vehicle‐induced wakes and provide practical design guidance for the deployment of guided VAWT arrays in highway environments.

title: FROM THERMAL ACCUMULATION TO HYBRID REGULATION: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF COOLING STRATEGIES IN PHOTOVOLTAIC AND PV/T SYSTEMS
authors: Karrar Jawad Hussein, Rana Ali Hussein
abstract: Both Photovoltaic (PV) and Photovoltaic/Thermal (PV/T) systems still remain significantly affected by thermal energy storage since around 70–80% of the sunlight absorbed turns into heat and not electricity. This leads to overheating and reduction of the systems' efficiency under hot weather conditions. The current research paper seeks to provide a critical review of some of the latest findings concerning thermal management solutions for PV and PV/T technologies while building a framework that connects cooling approaches to thermo-electrical performance. For the purpose of the research, a systematic analysis and comparison of more than 60 scientific papers, especially those written within the years 2022-2025, are considered alongside basic studies on the cooling of PV/T systems. Passive cooling includes methods such as using Phase Change Materials (PCMs). Active cooling technologies include air, water, and nanofluid cooling. Finally, hybrid solutions that involve PCMs and enhanced convective heat transfer are also studied. Comparative analysis shows that passive cooling with PCMs is relatively simple and highly efficient in terms of thermal energy storage while active cooling with nanofluids allows reaching up to 20 degrees centigrade decrease in temperatures and up to 15% efficiency improvement. In turn, hybrid solutions allow obtaining even better thermo-electrical efficiency at high levels of irradiation, up to 80%, due to up to 25°C temperature drop achieved in experiments. Yet, several challenges need to be addressed: pumping losses, nanofluids stability issues, PCMs performance in cycles, etc.

title: Techno-economic optimisation of grid-interactive hydropower with tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery
authors: Kanzumba Kusakana, Jakub Jurasz, Nsilulu Tresor Mbungu
abstract: The transition toward renewable energy systems increasingly requires solutions that improve energy efficiency while accounting for the coupled interaction between water resources, energy production, and economic performance. This study investigates a grid-interactive hydropower system enhanced with tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery as a means of improving water resource utilisation without major infrastructure modifications. By recovering residual kinetic energy from hydropower tailraces, the proposed configuration enables a combined-cycle hydropower system that exploits both the potential and kinetic energy of water. The main contribution of this work is the development of an integrated techno-economic optimisation framework that explicitly couples hydropower operation, tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery, reservoir dynamics, and grid interaction. A site-specific nonlinear relationship between hydropower outflow and tailrace flow velocity is derived from measurements and embedded directly into the optimisation model, allowing hydrokinetic power generation to be represented without simplified assumptions. Reservoir dynamics are further enhanced by incorporating evaporation and precipitation as exogenous variables, enabling the coupled behaviour of water availability, energy dispatch, and economic performance to be evaluated. Open-loop, closed-loop, and model predictive control strategies are formulated and comparatively assessed. Simulation results demonstrate that integrating hydrokinetic turbines into hydropower tailraces can achieve net energy savings of up to 63% and reduce net energy costs by approximately 61%, relative to a baseline grid-interactive hydropower system without hydrokinetic recovery under identical daily operating conditions and load demand. Annual analysis shows comparable trends, with savings remaining above 60% over the full-year horizon. Model predictive control provides the most robust operational performance by effectively aligning generation with demand while maintaining reservoir constraints. Economic analysis indicates that the cumulative operational savings generated by the hydrokinetic integration offset the initial hydrokinetic investment cost after approximately 1.1 years, while the overall discounted payback period is estimated at 2.88 years over the 20-year project horizon. The results confirm that tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery offers a scalable and economically attractive pathway for improving resource efficiency at the energy–water interface.

title: Highly Robust High-Order Numerical Framework for Solving Six-Equation Compressible Two-Phase Flow Model with Phase Change
authors: Qi-Chao Li, Lin Fu (Associate Professor)
abstract: The six-equation, single-velocity, two-phase flow model based on the diffuse-interface method (DIM) with stiff pressure relaxation has recently gained attention for its ability to handle metastable fluids, ensure robust positivity of volume fractions, and yield effective sound speeds consistent with Wood’s law. However, the presence of nonconservative terms in the phasic energy equations poses substantial challenges for numerical simulation, particularly in shock–interface interaction problems. In this work, we develop a general numerical framework for this model that achieves high fidelity, low dissipation, and strong robustness, while also accounting for phase change via additional source terms. First, we introduce a path-conservative Harten–Lax–van Leer–Contact (HLLC) solver grounded in Dal Maso–LeFloch–Murat (DLM) theory, enabling high-fidelity resolution of shock–interface interaction problems with phase change. This approach allows wave speeds to be captured more accurately, even in the presence of strong shock waves. Second, we propose a hybrid WENO–MOOD framework that combines high-resolution Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) schemes with a posteriori Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD), reducing numerical dissipation and enhancing robustness near dynamically generated interfaces. An improved MOOD technique, which limits phasic rather than mixture sound speed, enables the application of high-order WENO schemes to phase change problems. This approach allows for more accurate calculation of phase generation compared to traditional Monotone Upstream-centered Schemes for Conservation Laws (MUSCL), and significantly improves robustness when simulating phase change processes using high-order schemes. Third, by reformulating the mass transfer operator as a single nonlinear temperature equation, we further improve the relaxation method for phase change, enhancing robustness and reducing computational cost. A series of benchmark tests for compressible two-phase flows with phase transition demonstrate that WENO–MOOD delivers superior interface capturing and resolves more phase-change-induced flow structures than the conventional MUSCL scheme, while the improved relaxation method significantly reduces computational cost. This study provides a comprehensive assessment of numerical strategies for multiphase flow models and offers practical guidelines for the accurate and efficient simulation of phase-transition phenomena.

title: Goal-Oriented Weighting of Reynolds-Stress Data for Learning Turbulence Models in Complex Flows
authors: Zhuolin Zhao, Haochen Wang, Youngwoo Kim, Solkeun Jee, Heng Xiao
abstract: Abstract Data-driven turbulence models for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations offer a promising route to improving predictions of complex flows. Such models, specifically the turbulence constitutive relations, can be learned efficiently from high-fidelity Reynolds-stress data without evaluating the RANS equations during training. However, conventional losses weight all tensor-component and spatial errors equally, although their influence on a quantity of interest (QoI) can differ significantly; reducing the aggregate stress error therefore does not necessarily lead to an improved QoI prediction. Training against flow-level observations accounts for this dependence but requires repeated, potentially expensive RANS solutions. In canonical shear flows, physical reasoning can identify the shear component as the only one relevant for the mean-flow prediction. Motivated by this example, we propose a goal-oriented method to select and weight Reynolds-stress training data for complex flows. For a specified QoI, a single offline adjoint evaluation quantifies its sensitivity to local perturbations of each Reynolds-stress component. These sensitivities are converted into fixed weights in the supervised loss, enabling training without further RANS solutions. We validate the weighting in square-duct and periodic-hill flows, then apply it to a film-cooling jet in crossflow, where it improves velocity and cooling-effectiveness predictions over uniformly weighted training despite using a velocity-only QoI. Beyond turbulence modelling, this work suggests a broader strategy for aligning supervised learning with downstream prediction goals while preserving training efficiency.

title: 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics Modeling on Riverbed Scouring Caused by Pipeline Crossing
authors: Zahiraniza Mustaffa, Ebrahim Al-Qadami, Muhammad Amin Ahmad Rusli, Mohd Adib Mohammad Razi, Syed Muzzamil Hussain Shah
abstract: This chapter investigates sediment scour around underwater pipelines using 3D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling. A pipeline crossing a river was analyzed at three orientations relative to flow: 40° (Scenario 1), 70° (Scenario 2), and 90° (Scenario 3). Additionally, three gap conditions between the pipeline and riverbed were considered: −0.016 m (partially submerged, Case 1), 0 m (on the riverbed, Case 2), and 0.016 m (elevated, Case 3). Results showed no sediment scouring in Case 1, with sediment deposition occurring instead, reaching a maximum height of 0.01 m in Scenario 1. However, scouring was observed in Cases 2 and 3. The highest scour depth (0.021 m) 134 occurred in Scenario 2, Case 2, while the lowest (0.005 m) was in Scenario 1, Case 2. Flow velocity remained consistent across scenarios at approximately 2 m/s. The highest fluid pressure on the pipeline was observed in Scenario 1, likely due to its greater exposure to the flow. These findings highlight the influence of pipeline orientation and gap height on scour development, crucial for optimizing underwater pipeline installations.

title: Large-eddy simulation of shear-driven wake interactions in tandem wind turbines
authors: Abdelmalek Bouaziz, Radouan Boukharfane
abstract: The role of inflow shear in wind-turbine wake dynamics remains poorly understood, since it is difficult to disentangle shear effects from atmospheric turbulence in experimental and operational settings. In this work, high-fidelity large-eddy simulations with over 100 million grid cells, coupled with the actuator line method, are employed to investigate wake interactions between two aligned NREL-5MW turbines. To isolate shear-driven mechanisms in isolation from background turbulence effects, the study deliberately avoids modeling a fully developed atmospheric boundary layer and instead imposes controlled linear vertical shear profiles at the inlet. These profiles are derived from the classical power-law formulation while maintaining a fixed hub-height velocity across all simulations. The results show three primary effects of vertical shear: shear destabilizes the tip-vortex system, enhances turbulence production and streamwise Reynolds stresses, and imprints a persistent vertical asymmetry in the wake. Collectively, these effects accelerate wake recovery and substantially modify the inflow to the downstream turbine, resulting in increased power output (up to 11%) coupled with enhanced cyclic loading. These findings establish that vertical shear, independent of background turbulence, is a primary determinant of wake recovery and downstream turbine performance, with direct implications for high-fidelity wake modeling and wind-farm optimization.

title: High-Lift Prediction Workshop 5: Hybrid RANS/LES Technology Focus Group Summary
authors: Neil Ashton, Paul Batten, Andrew Cary, Kevin Holst, Vangelis Skaperdas
abstract: This study summarizes the work of the hybrid Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes/large-eddy simulation (HRLES) Technology Focus Group (TFG) for the 5th High-Lift Prediction Workshop (HLPW-5). Results indicate that, as shown in HLPW-4, HRLES methodologies continue to consistently outperform Spalart–Allmaras-based RANS models in predicting maximum lift coefficients ([Formula: see text]) and flowfield correlations for a range of high-lift aircraft geometry variations—from clean wings to those with flaps, slats, and engine nacelles. However, challenges persist in simulating low angle-of-attack configurations with deployed flaps, as well as the transitional flow in some of the lower-Reynolds-number cases studied. This work also highlights the importance of mesh resolution in achieving consistent results across different HRLES implementations. For test case 2.2, including deployed slats, lift-convergence trends indicate that meshes with at least approximately 175 million cells were needed to approach an asymptotic region; comparable convergence could not be demonstrated for all configurations and angles of attack. Code-to-code agreement was strongest for adequately resolved Spalart–Allmaras-delayed detached-eddy simulation-family submissions away from stall conditions. A single cost ratio relative to RANS could not be inferred from the workshop submissions, although representative HRLES calculations required tens of convective time units before collecting stationary statistics. While HRLES methods demonstrate promise for industrial applications, this work underscores the need for further research to enhance the maturity and widespread applicability of these methods.

title: From RANS Prediction to Hydrofoil Optimization: A Benchmark of Neural Surrogates
authors: Aarav Dixit
abstract: Abstract Neural flow surrogates are usually compared by field error, although their practical value often lies in the designs they select. We compare a convolutional neural network U-Net (CNN-U-Net), a physics-informed neural network (PINN), a Fourier neural operator (FNO), and a deep operator network (DeepONet) on 381 Open- FOAM computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils in water. Complete families form disjoint training, validation, and final-test sets, and every architecture is trained with three seeds. The models predict Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) fields, lift, drag, and pressure-based cavitation-inception risk, and then drive the same four-parameter hydrofoil shape-optimization loop. DeepONet gives the lowest mean pressure, Cp , lift, and drag errors on the untouched test families; the PINN is close and has the fastest inference. Inference is 384–665 times faster than OpenFOAM. Across seeds, endpoint solves give mean L/D from 22.10 to 37.47, but a three-level grid study shows that drag remains mesh-sensitive. Field accuracy, force accuracy, search quality, and simulator verification are related but not interchangeable.

authors: Pablo Echeverria Landín, Guillermo Guzmán Chávez
abstract: This study evaluates thermal comfort conditions in a social housing unit located in Quito, Ecuador, through the application of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations and passive design strategies. The research is based on a representative housing model constructed with conventional concrete and masonry systems, characterized by limited environmental performance. The methodology employs STAR-CCM+ software to analyze temperature distribution, airflow behavior, and indoor environmental quality indicators, specifically Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) and Predicted Percentage of Dissatisfied (PPD), in accordance with ISO 7730 standards. Four scenarios were assessed: baseline model, envelope improvement, implementation of wind-capturing systems, and optimization of building orientation and openings. The results demonstrate that interventions focused solely on the building envelope produce limited improvements, whereas integrated strategies combining natural ventilation and architectural design achieve a reduction in indoor temperature of up to 2 °C and a significant increase in the area of thermal comfort. The study confirms that thermal comfort in social housing depends on the interaction between materials, ventilation, and spatial configuration, providing a replicable approach for similar Andean contexts.

title: Artificial Neural Network Model to Enhance Thermal Prediction in Circular Porous Slider System With Pollutant Ejected by an External Source
authors: Prateek Kattimani, Vishwanatha Rajeev Banakar, Gudihindlar Kuberappa Tejaswini, Ballajja Chandrappa Prasannakumara
abstract: ABSTRACT Porous slider systems are widely relevant to lubrication, thermal management, and transfer processes where coupled fluid flow, heat transfer, and species transfer need to be controlled. Motivated by these applications, the present study examines the flow, thermal, and concentration characteristics of a fluid past a circular porous slider. The mathematical model incorporates nonlinear thermal radiation, heat generation/absorption, pollutant concentration, and magnetic‐field effects. Using appropriate similarity variables, the governing partial differential equations for velocity, temperature, and concentration are converted into nonlinear ordinary differential equations, which are numerically solved by utilizing the Lerch polynomial collocation method. Moreover, an artificial neural network model is employed to investigate the predictions of velocity, temperature, and concentration profiles. The results show that fluid flow is inhibited as the magnetic field strength increases due to the resistive Lorentz force, while the temperature profile increases substantially. The temperature and concentration profiles diminish with increasing Reynolds numbers as the thermal and concentration boundary layer thickness decreases. Additionally, the higher radiation and heat source/sink parameters enhance the temperature profile. The outcomes of the current article are essential for various types of porous lubrication systems, thermal management devices, pollutant control technologies, and industrial cooling processes.
