title: Physics-informed wavelet–Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics
authors: Chao Wang, Shilong Li, Yunpeng Wang, Tianbai Xiao, Zelong Yuan, Chenyue Xie, Chunyu Guo
abstract: Multiscale fluid flows often contain localized flow structures, such as viscous shock layers, wet–dry fronts, steady viscous wakes, decaying vortical structures, and vortex-shedding patterns, whose accurate prediction requires the simultaneous preservation of global conservation trends and small-scale gradients. This study examines these flow-physics requirements through a physics-informed wavelet–Fourier (PIWF) representation for multiscale fluid dynamics. Instead of relying on a monolithic neural approximator, the formulation separates two complementary components of the flow field within a physics-informed neural representation: long-range coherent modes through a Fourier-basis branch and localized steep-gradient or vortical features through a compactly supported wavelet branch. The outputs are fused with a residual multilayer perceptron using channel attention, and the governing equations, initial conditions, and boundary conditions are imposed directly through the physics-informed loss. The model is assessed on five canonical fluid-dynamics problems: Burgers' equation, the shallow water equations, Kovasznay flow, Taylor–Green vortex flow, and two-dimensional cylinder wake. The results show that PIWF improves the resolution of shock-like gradients, wet–dry interfaces, steady wake fields, decaying vortical structures, vorticity extrema, and broadband wake spectra relative to standard physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold networks. These findings indicate that a wavelet–Fourier physics-informed representation can provide a useful route for analyzing multiscale flow phenomena when high-fidelity interior reference data are limited or unavailable.

title: Component-Level Evaluation of Adaptive PINN Training for CFD-Oriented Crystal Growth Simulation
authors: Niruta Chapagain, Rohit Raj, Bertwin Kurisinkal Shine, Aditya A S
abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) training minimizes a weighted combination of partial differential equation (PDE), boundary-condition, and initial-condition losses. Because adaptive methods modify these weights during training, their weighted total losses are not always directly comparable. We compare fixed-weight PINN, gradient-normalized PINN (GNPINN), and a rule-based adaptive controller (AgenticPINN) under matched settings on a heat-equation benchmark and a simplified Czochralski-oriented thermal-fluid problem. In the crystal-growth MLP experiment, adaptive control reduced the PDE residual from the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, while the boundary-condition loss increased from the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$. On the heat-equation benchmark, GNPINN achieved the lowest relative $L_2$ field error (0.054), whereas AgenticPINN obtained the smallest PDE residual but a relative $L_2$ error of 1.368. Gaussian-process surrogates were additionally evaluated using case-wise holdout tests on corrected Czochralski CFD parameter sweeps. The temperature-field error for the temperature sweep was approximately 6%, whereas the axial-velocity error for the crystal-rotation sweep was approximately 42%. These findings show that adaptive control can improve equation satisfaction while weakening other physical constraints. PINN training should therefore be evaluated using separate PDE, boundary-condition, and solution-error metrics rather than weighted total loss alone.

title: Physics-informed neural network reconstructions of free surfaces and flow fields from sparse data in turbulent regimes, with applications in stirred tanks
authors: Ming Li Wong, Yuqing Feng, Peter J. Witt, Qixuan Zhu
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless framework for fluid dynamics, capable of solving both forward and inverse problems, and incorporating observational data into the model. However, their application to coupled multiphase turbulent flows remains limited, particularly in industrial inverse problems, where measurements may be sparse, expensive, and are often devoid of turbulence values. In this work, we develop a PINN framework for reconstructing the free surface, along with the velocity and pressure fields from sparse data, and test it on a mixing tank. Models are trained on limited velocity and pressure data from a time-averaged, axisymmetric CFD reference simulation. The data are free of direct measurements from the free surface or turbulence terms. Models are evaluated across varying impeller speeds and fluid viscosities. Both laminar and turbulent models are tested, including with eddy viscosity closures and anisotropic stresses. A Spalart–Allmaras turbulence closure is used, while including anisotropic stresses can improve the pressure and free surface predictions. From as few as 25 measurement locations, models are able to reconstruct, with low error, the velocity and pressure fields, and the final model achieves average free-surface errors below 1 mm in all tested operating conditions relative to a CFD reference. Additionally, models can accurately detect features such as additional vortices, jet splitting and impingement regions.

title: Path planning for logistics UAVs considering energy consumption and safety under wind field uncertainty
authors: Mingyang Li, Lichao Wang, Shulu Chen
abstract: Wind disturbances at low altitudes increase energy consumption and safety risks for multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in densely built urban environments. High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is too expensive for online path planning, while threshold methods represent hazardous regions as binary no-fly zones. This study proposes a path planning framework that combines a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate with a multiplicative cost model incorporating predictive uncertainty. The FNO predicts the urban wind field and its spatial uncertainty. The predicted wind field determines physical flight energy, while uncertainty modulates this term to form an equivalent energy cost. Costs for the 26-neighborhood are precomputed, allowing 3D A ∗ search through tensor lookups. Experiments use CFD wind fields for a 3D area modeled on the Macao Peninsula, five meteorological scenarios, and 13 valid delivery routes. Mean FNO inference time is 102.013 ms. After preprocessing and cost tensor construction, mean search time per route is 5.675 s. Mean risk exposure, defined as the percentage of path nodes above a predictive uncertainty threshold, decreases from 25.76% for Optimal Energy to 7.12% for the proposed method, with scenario values from 5.68% to 11.47%. Mean physical energy increases by 2.34% relative to Optimal Energy. Relative to geometric shortest path planning, energy decreases by 4.40% in the annual average scenario and by 5.25% in winter. The framework improves the balance between uncertainty exposure and modeled energy consumption, supporting potential applications in more sustainable urban logistics planning.

title: Electron-Mediated Transport in Space, Astrophysical, and Laboratory Plasmas
authors: Jesse T. Coburn, Maria Elena Innocenti, Daniel Verscharen, Anton V. Artemyev, Jasper S Halekas, Wence Jiang, Matthew W. Kunz, M. J. Pueschel, Mario Riquelme, Š. Štverák, Lynn B. Wilson III
abstract: Electron-mediated transport is fundamental to the thermal and dynamical evolution of plasmas across a vast range of physical environments, from the solar wind and solar atmosphere to astrophysical systems such as galaxy clusters and accretion flows, to laboratory and fusion plasmas. This article reviews the current state of understanding of electron transport, drawing together observations, simulations, and theory to contextualise key challenges and open questions. We characterise plasma environments using the Knudsen number and electron beta, and highlight that some systems fall in an intermediate regime between the collisional and collisionless limits. In the collisional limit, transport is well described by the Chapman-Enskog-Braginskii framework, yielding anisotropic heat fluxes and momentum transfer rates governed by the ratio of the electron mean free path to the electron gyroradius. In the collisionless limit, Landau-fluid closures and quasilinear wave-particle interaction theory describe heat flux regulation through resonant instabilities, particularly whistler-mode waves, which suppress parallel electron heat flux below Spitzer-Härm predictions in high-beta plasmas. We review approaches to bridging collisional and collisionless regimes, including velocity-space-dependent collision operators, moment-based interpolating closures, and data-driven methods trained on fully kinetic simulations. Comparison with solar wind observations from the Parker Solar Probe and Wind missions reveals that the current attempts at bridging collisional and collisionless closures account for only limited regions of parameter space, underscoring the need for improved models. Four central challenges are identified for future transport theory: capturing the velocity-space dependence of collisional and collisionless scattering, describing spatial transitions between transport regimes, incorporating turbulence, and developing computationally tractable effective collision operators for large-scale simulations.

title: Interfacial turbulence damping effect on the melt pool dimensions and surface topology during powder bed fusion additive manufacturing
authors: Gaius Chukwuka Nzebuka, Chukwuzubelu Okenwa Ufodike, Lucky Ekene Bernard
abstract: A physics-based melt pool turbulence model for a multiphase flow was developed to study the effect of turbulence in a powder-based fusion additive manufacturing process. Two-equation eddy viscosity model which include the Realizable k-ε and the Shear Stress Transport (SST)- k-ω were selected to quantify the turbulence level in the melt pool of powder bed fusion under no interfacial damping. The performance of the two turbulence models was assessed based on their ability to better predict the melt pool dimensions. Further, the interfacial turbulence damping was activated for the best-performing turbulence model to analyze its effect on the melt pool surface topology and dimensions. Assessment of the turbulence level using the turbulent viscosity ratio shows a high turbulence production in the melt pool, and it affects the melt pool dimensions. The analysis shows that the SST- k-ω model’s prediction of the melt pool performs better than the Realizable k-ε model. Subsequent simulations revealed that the interfacial turbulence damping affects the melt pool surface topology and melt pool dimensions. Without interfacial damping, the turbulent viscosity ratio is eleven times greater than its molecular values. An increase in the interfacial damping coefficient decreases the turbulence viscosity ratio, increases the backward flow along the interface, and decreases the melt depth and width. The study reveals new knowledge in the melt pool flow structure, which may be useful for better process control of the powder bed fusion additive manufacturing processes.

title: Discretization-based reconstruction of watertight building geometry from raw GIS data for urban CFD simulation
authors: Jinwoo Choi, Taehoon Hong, Hyeonggyun Kim, Kwangbok Jeong
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban wind simulations require CFD-ready building geometries, yet real-world GIS datasets often contain geometric inconsistencies that hinder automated preprocessing and mesh generation. This study presents an automated geometry generation pipeline that converts heterogeneous GIS building data into watertight LOD1 models suitable for urban CFD applications. The workflow combines topology-neutral surface sampling, footprint reconstruction, geometry simplification, and automated regularization within a single preprocessing framework. A district-scale case study of approximately 15,000 buildings in Seoul was used to evaluate geometry quality, fidelity, and computational efficiency. The generated models achieved 100% watertightness while preserving building-scale geometric characteristics with median volume fidelity and footprint IoU values of 0.994 and 0.992, respectively. Compared with manual preprocessing workflows, the proposed approach reduced processing time from several days to approximately 190 seconds. The framework provides a practical foundation for scalable generation of CFD-ready urban geometries, supporting future large-scale airflow simulations and data-driven modeling.

title: Learning to Learn in Manufacturing: Bayesian Meta-Learning for Design Transferability
authors: Aditya Rane, Paritosh Ramanan, Srikanthan Ramesh, Akash Deep
abstract: The shift toward mass personalization in manufacturing demands data-efficient methods for adapting design and process models to diverse, individualized requirements. However, the limited transferability of process knowledge and reliance on costly trial-and-error procedures hinder scalability. This work investigates Bayesian meta-learning as a framework for improving knowledge transfer across related design optimization tasks. We apply the PAC-Optimal Hyper-Posterior (PACOH) framework to learn a distribution of Gaussian process priors from historical tasks referred to as hyper priors. This approach provides principled PAC-Bayesian guarantee against meta-overfitting and avoids complex bi-level optimization problem seen in traditional methods, making it ideal for “few-task” and “few-samples” manufacturing scenarios. Using an airfoil design optimization case study, we evaluate the framework’s transferability, scalability, and robustness under data corruption. Our results demonstrate that meta-learned priors enable a smarter starting point that leverages task-based similarity and rapidly optimizes new unseen tasks in just 2-6 iterations. This eventually provides a 5-fold improvement over scenarios where tasks are designed in isolation and modeled with standard per-task learning (i.e., no meta-learning). This framework successfully generalizes to a new class of airfoils and maintains high performance even when trained on corrupted data, demonstrating its robustness. Overall, the proposed Bayesian meta-learning framework provides a sample-efficient and transferable solution for learning-to-learn in high-mix manufacturing.

title: Thermal Energy Optimization of Nanofluid Movement in Spinning Porous Tubes Through Neural Networks
authors: Yasir Iqbal, Qazi Mahmood Ul Hassan, Raymond Ghandour, Julien Moussa H. Barakat, Zaher Al Barakeh
abstract: Objective: The current study combines artificial intelligence (AI) with mathematical modeling to analyze nanofluid flow behavior, convective heat transfer, and thermal radiation in a rotating permeable channel. Methods/Analysis: Governing equations are derived for a CuO-water nanofluid using its thermo-physical properties, bulk conditions, and nondimensional variables; the partial differential equations are reduced to ordinary differential equations (ODEs) through similarity transformations, and the resulting boundary value problem (BVP) is solved using a shooting technique coupled with the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method to generate the reference dataset. The Feedforward Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) Artificial Neural Network (ANN), trained with the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm (LMA), is then developed as an optimized surrogate model. Findings: The effects of the Reynolds number, magnetic parameter, suction/injection, rotation parameter, and Grashof number on the velocity and temperature distributions are interpreted through computational simulations and graphical analysis. The ANN model attains very low mean squared error, near-unity regression, and small gradients, confirming convergence and high predictive accuracy. Novelty: By integrating an ANN surrogate with the rotating permeable-channel nanofluid model, this study contributes to AI-computational methods in fluid mechanics and applied mathematics, offering value to both academic research and engineering practice.

title: Experimentally validated hybrid CFD-machine learning framework for predicting hydrogen evolution reaction performance of Ba0.5Ca0.5CoO3 perovskite electrocatalyst
authors: Elham Fattahi, Dina I. Bakranova, Elham Mahmoudi, Amin Sokhansanj, Nurlan Bakranov, Ali Çoruh, Nagihan Çaylak Delibaş, Ergün Nart, Elnaz Asghari, Aligholi Niaei
abstract: Accurate prediction of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance under varying operating conditions conventionally requires extensive electrochemical measurements or computationally intensive simulations. To address this challenge, an experimentally validated framework integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and machine learning (ML) was developed for mechanistic analysis and HER performance prediction of Ba 0.5 Ca 0.5 CoO 3 perovskite electrocatalyst. A 3D multiphysics CFD model was established by coupling fluid flow, electrochemical kinetics, and ionic transport. The simulated polarization curves showed good agreement with experimental measurements across a wide range of temperatures (25-65°C) and electrolyte concentrations (1-5 M KOH). The validated CFD model was subsequently used to generate a comprehensive dataset for training three ML models, namely Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Ensemble Learning. All developed models demonstrated excellent predictive capability, achieving R 2 > 0.985, with GPR slightly outperforming the other models by showing a narrower error distribution. The GPR model was further employed to predict HER current density at previously unseen operating conditions. It exhibited strong agreement with CFD predictions under the sampled operating conditions (R 2 > 0.998), demonstrating robust interpolation capability and its potential as a computationally efficient surrogate for CFD simulations. Furthermore, permutation feature importance (PFI) analysis identified applied potential as the most influential operating parameter for predicting HER current density. The proposed hybrid CFD-ML framework enables rapid and computationally efficient prediction of the experimentally anchored CFD response within the investigated operating domain.

title: Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition for Operator Learning
authors: Peng Shi, Li-Ming Zhang, Tao Qian, Stephen Tierney, Jie Yin, Jun-Bin Gao
abstract: Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) offer an efficient paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, FNOs rely on a fixed Fourier basis and hard frequency truncation, which inherently limit their ability to model non-periodic, localized, and fine-scale solution structures. We propose the Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition Neural Operator (SAFDNO), a spectral neural operator that replaces predefined Fourier modes with an adaptive Takenaka-Malmquist (TM) orthonormal system derived from the theory of Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition (SAFD). Instead of performing an expensive greedy pole search in classical SAFD, SAFDNO amortizes stochastic pole selection through a neural pole predictor and constructs the adaptive TM system directly from latent features. The resulting operator performs learned filtering on coefficients of analytic branches in the Hardy space with respect to the input-adaptive TM system, preserving the global receptive field of spectral operators while providing a more flexible representation than using fixed spectral bases. Across nine PDE benchmark problems, SAFDNO achieves the best performance on all six regular-grid problems among strong neural operator baselines, with especially notable gains on Darcy, Burgers, and Navier-Stokes, where fixed Fourier modes are often less effective at modeling localized oscillations, sharp transitions, and multiscale structures. SAFDNO also exhibits stronger zero-shot super-resolution performance and shows less performance degradation when deployed on finer discretizations. These results suggest that the input-adaptive TM system provides a promising alternative to fixed spectral representations for neural operator learning.

title: Only Linear Constraints Survive Coarse-Graining: Evaluating Physics-Constrained Neural Operators on Stochastically Forced Turbulence
authors: Michael Groom, Rafael Oliveira
abstract: A physics-informed loss adds a discretised PDE residual to the data term, but is only strictly valid if the equations being enforced are closed on the fields being fitted. This fails on coarse-grained, stochastically forced data: nonlinear terms in the PDE generally do not commute with the filter, so the coarse-grained fields do not satisfy the original equations, and driving their residual to zero encodes an implicit closure into the learned operator. Under normalised, translation-invariant filtering on a periodic domain, constant-coefficient linear constraints remain valid on the filtered grid. For the 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, two such constraints are continuity and global momentum balance. We enforce these exactly by applying a closed-form projection on the output of a Fourier neural operator (FNO) at $O(N \log N)$ cost. On two-dimensional isotropic turbulence, truncated so that its forcing lies entirely beyond the cutoff wavenumber, the projection achieves a continuity error of $5.0\times10^{-7}$ against 0.51 for a plain FNO and 0.17 for a physics-informed FNO, and a global momentum balance error of $8.6\times10^{-11}$ against $7.5\times10^{-4}$ and $8.3\times10^{-4}$. The projection only costs an extra 2% of training time, and takes the fraction of rollouts whose energy remains bounded at 448 steps from 0.18 to 0.87. On resolved Kolmogorov flow, test-time optimisation costs approximately 3,300$\times$ as much per trajectory as the projection, while leaving maximum divergence three orders of magnitude higher. Nonlinear constraints can also be enforced once their unclosed terms are modelled: closing the global energy balance with a constant subgrid flux, fitted from the coarse training data alone, removes the 20.9% energy deficit that enforcing the unclosed balance produces and keeps every free-running rollout bounded over 2,000 steps.

title: Computational Fluid Dynamics Simulation of an Unbaffled Stirred Tank Using Sliding Mesh Model
authors: Sibin V Mathew, K Supradeepan, P Sankar Ganesh
abstract: Stirred tanks are widely used in renewable energy systems like anaerobic digestion, where adequate mixing of organic slurry and microbes is essential for enhancing biogas production. The current study used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to assess the flow behaviour in an unbaffled tank agitated by a Rushton impeller. The tank is open at the top and partially filled with water beneath an air zone. The flow turbulence and the air-water interface in the tank are described by the Reynolds Stress Model (RSM) and Volume of Fluid (VOF) model, respectively. The Sliding Mesh (SM) model, which divides the computational domain into rotating and stationary zones, was used to capture the impeller motion. The rotating zone size is optimised by reducing the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of the simulated and experimental free surface profiles. The optimised rotating zone size is used for evaluating the free surface profile, power number, flow number, and mean velocity components, at 139, 194, and 240 rpm. The free surface profiles for various impeller speeds intersect on a point located at a critical radius from the stirred tank axis. The tangential velocity dominates the flow domain, and create a swirling flow inside the tank. The swirling flow and lower axial velocity magnitude indicate weaker axial agitation. The power and flow numbers show a slight decrease with increasing Reynolds number, agreeing with the numerical and experimental results reported in the literature. The present work emphasizes the critical role of rotating zone dimensions in the SM approach for numerical accuracy. It delivers key insights into the complex hydrodynamics of an unbaffled stirred tank for renewable energy applications.

title: Review in coronary functional evaluation methods: applications of computational fluid dynamics and artificial intelligence in the context of coronary artery disease
authors: Haojia Qu, Peiqi Lou, Yibin Pan, Debao Guan, Tianqi Wang, Hao Xu, Xiaorong Chen, Xinyang Ge
abstract: Coronary artery disease, driven by the progressive accumulation of atherosclerotic plaque within the epicardial coronary arteries, remains a leading cause of myocardial ischemia and global morbidity. A fundamental challenge in the clinical management of the disease has been the reliance on anatomic stenosis severity alone, a metric that frequently dissociates from the hemodynamic significance of a lesion and thus offers limited guidance for optimal revascularization. The advent of invasive measurements marked a transformative paradigm shift, enabling the development of a diverse functional indices for the evaluation of coronary physiology. Recently, the development of computational science and artificial intelligence has accelerated the translation of these physiological assessments into the non-invasive domain, primarily through high-fidelity numerical simulations and efficient machine learning algorithms. This review systematically examines the evolution of coronary functional assessment across several pivotal frontiers. It begins by contextualizing the diagnostic landscape prior to the widespread adoption of functional indices, where clinical decisions were predominantly informed by imaging-derived anatomical parameters. Subsequently, it traces the historical evolution of invasive coronary functional indices, critically evaluating the comparative effectiveness of pressure-derived metrics against flow-derived metrics in the detection of hemodynamically significant ischemia. Furthermore, a critical evaluation of emerging artificial intelligence methodologies for the non-invasive evaluation of functional significance were employed. By synthesizing these technological methodologies, this review aims to elucidate the appropriate clinical application of each functional index, thereby providing a road-map for clinicians to achieve precise, individualized ischemia evaluation and guide therapeutic decision-making in the contemporary era of precision cardiovascular medicine.

title: Machine learning based optimization of UAV wing aerodynamics in the Martian environment
authors: Saumya Mathur, Suruchi Gupta, Devdeep Singh, Harshit Shukla
abstract: Mars exploration requires aerial platforms capable of overcoming the mobility limitations of orbiters and surface rovers. However, the extremely thin Martian atmosphere produces chord-based Reynolds numbers of 103–105 and a reduced speed of sound, making compressibility effects significant even at moderate flight velocities, leading to laminar separation, reduced lift, and nonlinear stall behavior that complicate rotor airfoil design. This study presents a hybrid Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Machine Learning (ML) framework for analysing rotor-wing airfoil performance under Martian conditions. A validated aerodynamic database was generated using structured-mesh CFD simulations across representative Reynolds numbers, Mach numbers, and angles of attack for multiple NACA airfoils. Performance metrics including CL/CD and $$C_{L}^{3/2} /C_{D}$$ were used to identify efficient configurations. Supervised regression models, including Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Gradient Boosting, and Neural Networks, were trained on the CFD dataset to develop fast surrogate predictors. The results demonstrate that the ML models accurately reproduce CFD trends while significantly reducing computational cost. Furthermore, a Physics-Guided Neural Network (PGNN) framework was implemented to enforce physically consistent predictions. The developed surrogate models are applicable only to the NACA 4-digit airfoil family investigated in this study and within the operating conditions considered (Re = 6000, Mach = 0.5 and a freestream turbulence intensity of 5%). Their applicability to other airfoil geometries or operating conditions requires further investigation. The proposed CFD–ML–PGNN workflow provides a scalable framework for efficient aerodynamic analysis and optimization of Martian UAV rotor airfoils.

title: Physics-informed Fourier basis neural network for fluid mechanics
authors: Chao Wang, Shilong Li, Zelong Yuan, Chunyu Guo
abstract: Conventional machine learning approaches struggle to capture periodic patterns and solve quasi-periodic boundary problems in fluid mechanics. This study proposes a physics-informed Fourier basis neural network (PIFBNN) that integrates adaptive Fourier series with physical constraints to address canonical partial differential equations. The architecture preserves Fourier series’ natural mathematical compatibility with periodic phenomena while incorporating trainable parameters (angular frequencies and weight coefficients) that enhance basis function flexibility and nonlinear learning capacity. We evaluate the framework on six fundamental fluid dynamics benchmarks: two-dimensional cylinder wake flow, lid-driven cavity flow, Kovasznay flow, Helmholtz equation, Burgers equation, and Allen-Cahn equation. The results indicate that PIFBNN is most effective for periodic and strongly oscillatory solutions; for smooth or weakly periodic cases, the error reduction relative to a standard physics-informed neural network (PINN) is more case dependent. In the additional four-model comparisons with PINN, physics-informed sinusoidal representation network (PISIREN), and physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN) under the same depth and total hidden width, PIFBNN uses fewer trainable parameters than the other three compared models and gives lower relative errors in most of the reported additional baseline tests. Sparse-data reconstruction and activation-function tests further show that the Fourier basis neural network (FBNN) captures periodic structure more effectively than a conventional artificial neural network (ANN) and is less sensitive to the activation function used in its fully connected branch. These results identify the solution regimes for which the proposed Fourier representation is most appropriate, while also showing that its effect is problem dependent.

title: A generative diffusion framework for physically consistent 3D turbulence
authors: Tianyi Li, Michele Buzzicotti, Fabio Bonaccorso, Luca Biferale
abstract: Abstract Synthesizing fully developed three-dimensional turbulence remains a long-standing problem in fluid mechanics and an open challenge for generative modeling. This difficulty arises from extreme dimensionality, multiscale fluctuations, strong intermittency, and the need to satisfy exact physical constraints, including incompressibility and prescribed mass and momentum fluxes under given boundary conditions. We propose a physics-constrained diffusion model in which some a priori constraints can be incorporated directly into the generative dynamics. Using rotating turbulence as a paradigmatic system with key geophysical applications, we assess the proposed framework. Here, we show that it enables stable and statistically faithful single-time synthesis of inertial-range three-dimensional turbulent velocity fields, accurately reproducing anisotropic energy spectra, intermittent statistics, and physical constraints, whereas standard denoising diffusion probabilistic models exhibit multiscale statistical deviations, violations of physical consistency, and substantially slower training convergence, thereby pointing to broader implications for generative modeling of high-dimensional, physically constrained complex systems.

title: Adaptive Explainable Machine Learning-Assisted High-Order Numerical Framework for Engineering Differential Equations
authors: Amarender Reddy Kommula, Venkata Manikanta Batchu
abstract: Engineering differential equations are widely used to model physical processes such as heat transfer, fluid flow, structural analysis, and wave propagation.High-order numerical methods provide accurate solutions, but their performance depends on selecting suitable computational parameters, including mesh size, polynomial order, and time-step size.In many practical applications, this process requires expert knowledge and repeated trial-and-error.This paper presents an adaptive explainable machine learning framework that supports high-order numerical methods through intelligent and transparent parameter selection.The proposed approach monitors the numerical solution, estimates local errors, and recommends adaptive refinement while explaining the reasons behind each decision.Unlike conventional black-box models, the framework combines data-driven learning with numerical error indicators to improve both accuracy and interpretability.The proposed framework is designed for a wide range of engineering applications and provides a practical approach to improving computational efficiency while reducing manual parameter tuning.It also offers a foundation for developing reliable and explainable numerical solvers for future scientific and engineering applications.

title: Control and Optimization of Thermal Transport in Unsteady Thin Film Flow of Aggregating Micropolar Nanofluids
authors: Syed Modassir Hussain, Margaret J. Johnson, Umair Khan, Adebowale Martins Obalalu
abstract: The increasing demand for industrial development, efficient energy utilization, and cost reduction has motivated extensive research into nanomaterials and radiative heat transfer. This study investigates the thermal transport characteristics of an aggregating micropolar nanofluid in unsteady thin film flow, considering the effects of variable viscosity and thermal conductivity. The working fluid consists of molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) nanoparticles dispersed in ethylene glycol, with the nanoparticle volume fraction varied over the range of 0–5%. The influences of radiative heat transfer, electromagnetic effects, spin gradient viscosity, electric field, and microinertia are examined for both aggregating (Agg) and non-aggregating (W-Agg) nanofluids. The Krieger–Dougherty and Maxwell–Bruggeman models are employed to characterize the effective viscosity and thermal conductivity, respectively, particularly at higher nanoparticle concentrations. The governing equations are transformed into a dimensionless system of coupled nonlinear differential equations and solved using the Chebyshev collocation method. The effects of the governing thermofluidic parameters on velocity, entropy generation, skin friction coefficient, and heat transfer rate are systematically analyzed. The results show that fluid velocity increases with increasing spin gradient viscosity and electric field strength for both Agg and W-Agg nanofluids. In the absence of nanoparticle aggregation, the shear stress decreases by approximately 0.35%, whereas the heat transfer gradient increases by about 3.13%. Furthermore, nanoparticle aggregation produces measurable changes in velocity and entropy generation, highlighting its important role in momentum and thermal transport. These findings demonstrate the potential of electromagnetic and micropolar effects for controlling thermal transport and improving the performance of nanofluid-based thin film systems.

title: Integrated air quality assessment using monitoring data, emission inventory, and aermod dispersion modeling: a case study of Sohar Port and Freezone, Oman
authors: Mohammed Ambu-Saidi, Yavari Zeinab, Mohammad Reza Nikoo
abstract: Industrial and port areas require integrated air quality assessment methods combining monitoring observations, meteorological conditions and atmospheric dispersion modeling. In this study, we have investigated the pollution behavior and industrial source contributions in the Sohar Port and Freezone industrial area of Oman for a multi-year period of ambient air quality monitoring data and meteorological observations and AERMOD dispersion modeling results for PM 10 , NO 2 , SO 2 and CO. All the pollutants were compared according to their dominant source properties, atmospheric behaviour and importance to industrial air quality management. The model performance was evaluated using fractional bias, normalized mean square error, index of agreement, geometric mean bias, geometric variance and predicted to observed concentration ratios. PM 10 concentrations were strongly influenced by regional background dust and resuspension processes, whereas NO 2 and SO 2 were more closely related to combustion and industrial point sources. The validation results for PM 10 and SO 2 were better agreed on than for NO 2 and CO. The results were affected by uncertainty regarding background concentrations, fugitive and traffic emissions, completeness of emission inventory and monitoring site representation. The study provides a practical and regionally relevant approach to assessing industrial air quality in arid coastal environments. The findings indicate the importance of improving emission inventories, characterizing background pollution in the region, accounting for fugitive and traffic pollution and optimization of monitoring infrastructure to help in sustainable industrial development and evidence-based air quality management.

title: Coupled aero-structural-electrical modeling and sensitivity analysis of a bladeless resonant wind turbine with hybrid energy harvesting
authors: Alexis León-Real-Flores, Leonardo Urbiola-Soto, Ricardo Yáñez-Valdez
abstract: Abstract Bladeless resonant wind turbines are an alternative technology for small-scale wind energy harvesting because they convert vortex-induced structural oscillations into electrical power without rotating blades. However, their efficiency is strongly affected by the coupled interaction between wake dynamics, structural vibration and energy harvesting. This work presents a reduced-order aero-structural-electrical model for a bladeless resonant wind turbine with hybrid electromagnetic–piezoelectric energy harvesting. The wake dynamics are represented using a Van der Pol-type oscillator, while the structural subsystem is modeled as an equivalent mast-beam cantilever system governed by the first Euler–Bernoulli bending mode. An effective modal mass formulation is incorporated to account for the modal participation of the continuous mast-beam system. The electromagnetic harvester is coupled to the mechanical equation through the induced current and the corresponding electromagnetic reaction force. The piezoelectric contribution is represented through an equivalent damping term and an associated harvested-power expression, so that the energy extracted by the piezoelectric subsystem is also reflected in the mechanical response. The novelty of the proposed framework lies in the integration of nonlinear wake dynamics, effective-modal structural behavior, electromagnetic mechanical feedback, equivalent piezoelectric energy extraction, and energetic admissibility criteria within a single reduced-order model for regime-conditioned performance assessment. A parametric sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the influence of aerodynamic, structural and harvesting variables on the lock-in condition, vibration response, harvested power and overall conversion efficiency. Energetic acceptance criteria were applied to avoid non-physical results in which the harvested electrical power exceeded the available wind power or the mechanical power transferred to the structural coordinate. Within the prescribed parameter domain and energetic acceptance criteria, the maximum model-predicted accepted efficiencies were approximately 24.50% in pre-resonance, 43.62% in resonance, and 42.70% in post-resonance. These values represent reduced-order numerical predictions normalized by the configuration-specific projected wind-power input and should not be interpreted as experimentally validated efficiencies. The dominant variables changed with the operating regime: the Strouhal number, cylinder density and vortex saturation were most relevant in pre-resonance; the number of electromagnetic generators, load resistance, coupling factor, electromagnetic coefficient and cylinder stiffness dominated in resonance; and the number of electromagnetic generators, coupling factor, cylinder diameter, cylinder stiffness and equivalent piezoelectric damping were the most influential variables in post-resonance. These results show that the efficiency of bladeless resonant wind turbines cannot be assessed from isolated component models, since mast geometry, modal structural properties, wake parameters and harvesting coefficients modify both the available mechanical energy and the electromechanical damping. The proposed model provides a preliminary design tool for identifying dominant variables before experimental prototyping or high-fidelity numerical simulations.

title: Spatiotemporal variability and hydrological interactions of inter-basin groundwater flow in 36 major river basins worldwide
authors: Luyao Ren, Xiankui Zeng, Dong Wang, Jichun Wu
abstract: Abstract. Inter-basin groundwater flow (IGF) transfers water across watershed boundaries and interacts with surface hydrological processes. However, the spatiotemporal characteristics of IGF in major river basins worldwide and its key role in the hydrological cycle remain unclear. Here, we reconstructed IGF time series for 36 major global basins. The results show that the absolute magnitude of the multi-year mean IGF exceeded 20 % of precipitation in nearly half of the basins. Neighboring basins show similar seasonal patterns of IGF, reflecting the response of lateral groundwater flow to climatic seasonality. More importantly, in almost all basins, the rapid response of IGF to precipitation is consistent with pressure propagation through groundwater systems. In half of the basins, IGF could serve as an external water source supporting evapotranspiration. These findings demonstrate that IGF is a critical link in the hydrological cycle. Neglecting IGF may introduce structural biases into the representation of hydrological processes and thus reduce the reliability of climate-change projections based on Earth system models.

title: Mesoscale numerical modelling of freeze–thaw deformation in closed- and open-system soils using a Voronoi–Delaunay lattice
authors: Zarghaam Haider Rizvi, Mohammad Arsalan Khan, Frank Wuttke
abstract: Freeze–thaw deformation in frost-susceptible soils couples heat transfer, phase change, water redistribution and irreversible thaw deformation. This study develops an axisymmetric Voronoi–Delaunay lattice framework with a finite-element-analysis-program (FEAP)-compatible residual–tangent organization, embedded displacement-jump histories and a bounded temperature-dependent creep law. Delaunay edges carry normal–shear interactions, while a circumcentric dual supplies transport faces and storage volumes. The global benchmark implementation combines apparent-heat-capacity heat transfer, a reduced total-water redistribution equation and fixed-reference small-strain lattice mechanics; it is not a complete Darcy-flow, effective-stress or discrete ice-lens formulation. Verification against radial conduction, Stefan-front propagation and confined compression produced errors of 1.45%, 3.53% and 5.88%, respectively. First-cycle heave and thaw-settlement endpoints from one closed Kieler Förde test and six independent open-system tests were used for case-level calibration. The calibrated model reproduced those endpoints with a median absolute percentage error of 0.36%. The subsequent Kieler Förde cycle trend was assessed without further endpoint calibration, and the FEAP jump–creep enrichment retained a median endpoint error of 3.03% without re-optimisation. Predicted temperature, ice fraction, total water, pressure proxy and displacement fields are reported as model outputs because co-registered water-content profiles, pore pressures and freezing-front positions were not available for every case. Four CPU workers produced a measured 3.25-fold batch speedup; an optional GPU sparse-solver route is supplied with deterministic CPU fallback. The framework is therefore intended for rapid laboratory-scale displacement assessment, while finite-strain kinematics and fully coupled ice-lens poromechanics remain future developments.

title: Image-based deep learning prediction of water entry flow pattern evolution for cross-domain vehicles
authors: Yuqing Hou, Jiale Yan, Yu Ao, Chaowu Sheng, Jiawang Chen
abstract: The water entry process of cross-domain vehicles (CDVs) involves complex nonlinear hydrodynamics, making rapid and accurate prediction challenging. Conventional CFD-based analyses are often computationally expensive for rapid design iterations, and experimental approaches face challenges in environmental control and sensor precision. This study develops a U-shaped Network with Multi-Head Attention (UN-MHA) framework for rapid image-based prediction of water entry flow pattern evolution. The framework takes consecutive experimental images as input and predicts the subsequent flow pattern snapshot, including cavity morphology, free-surface deformation, and wake evolution. A feature fusion enhancement module and multi-head attention mechanisms are introduced to improve multiscale feature representation and preserve interfacial details. The model is validated against experimental datasets covering both low-speed and high-speed water entry regimes. For the low-speed condition, the proposed UN-MHA achieves an MSE of 3.91 × 1 0 − 5 , a PSNR of 43.52 dB, and an SSIM of 0.992, outperforming several representative baseline models. The framework requires only 0.232 s for a single frame prediction. Under the high-speed condition, it maintains robust predictive performance, with MSE values ranging from 2 × 1 0 − 5 to 8 × 1 0 − 5 , and PSNR values between 34 and 38 dB. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides an accurate and computationally efficient approach for rapid prediction of transient water-entry flow patterns.

title: AI-Accelerated Gyrokinetic Predictions of Turbulent Transport for Stellarator Design Optimization and Experimental Planning
authors: R. Michael Churchill, Matt Landreman, Jong Youl Choi, Byoungchan Jang, Rory Conlin, Noah Mandell, Anima Anandkumar, Valentin Duruisseaux, Jeffrey Larson, Dario Panici, Yigit Gunsur Elmacioglu, Jai Sachdev, Tony Qian
abstract: Abstract Previous work built AI-based surrogates for a nonlinear gyrokinetic simulation code with the goal of using them for fast, direct calculations of turbulent ion heat flux in stellarator design optimizations and scenario planning for experiments. These AI surrogates were trained on data from \textgreater{}200k nonlinear, adiabatic electron gyrokinetic simulations with the gyrokinetic flux-tube code GX, using a wide range of stellarator magnetic configurations ($\sim$23k), positions in the plasma, and gradient scale lengths. In this paper, we demonstrate the use of the AI-based turbulence surrogate in the optimization of stellarator magnetic equilibrium and to speed up stellarator transport solvers. Due to its speed ($\sim${}ms), the AI-based surrogate enables previously unattainable optimization objectives, such as full radial profiles of ion turbulent heat flux, or directly optimizing to maximize the turbulent critical gradient at multiple locations across the plasma. These direct calculations provide a potentially more accurate optimization target and reduce reliance on ad-hoc heuristics that may not accurately capture the variation of turbulent transport with magnetic configuration. By including the AI-based surrogate for turbulent heat flux in a transport solver, we can quickly postprocess and confirm the improved ion temperature resulting from the optimized equilibrium. Finally, we demonstrate the use of AI agents with strong reasoning AI models to automate the outer loop, exploring many objective and hyperparameter configurations with this AI-based turbulence surrogate to discover improved turbulence optimized magnetic equilibria.

title: Agentic AI for Computational Fluid Dynamics: A Review
authors: Keonhak Lee, Innyoung Kim
abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) workflows remain strongly dependent on expert decisions in geometry preparation, meshing, model and solver configuration, convergence assessment, post-processing, and design iteration. This review examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) for CFD automation and engineering design, with emphasis on reinforcement learning (RL) agents and large language model (LLM) agents. RL agents provide rapid, task-specific, and physics-aware execution within predefined observation and action spaces, whereas LLM agents offer flexible goal interpretation, knowledge access, planning, and tool orchestration. To organize these potentially complementary capabilities, a unified taxonomy is introduced based on decision paradigm, CFD role, and degree of autonomy, while multi-agent organization is treated as a separate architectural property. The reviewed evidence indicates that neither RL nor LLM agents alone are sufficient for trustworthy autonomous CFD. A hierarchical autonomous-CFD-engineer architecture is therefore proposed, combining an LLM orchestrator, domain-specialized agents, conventional CFD tools, independent numerical and physical verification, shared provenance, and human governance. Extending this architecture toward hypothesis formulation, numerical-experiment design, and model discovery suggests a pathway to an AI CFD scientist; however, current systems support bounded automation and supervised scientific collaboration rather than independent scientific judgment.

title: Interpretable Multifidelity Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Spatiotemporal Nuclear Reactor Flow Modeling
authors: Meredith Eaheart, Majdi I Radaideh
abstract: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of nuclear reactor systems are computationally expensive, motivating machine learning methods that reduce cost while preserving accuracy. Multifidelity surrogate modeling addresses this by combining inexpensive low-fidelity data with limited high-fidelity data. This work investigates whether the high-fidelity data required to predict the spatiotemporal mass flow rate across all 193 fuel assemblies of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) core can be reduced, comparing black-box multifidelity feedforward neural networks (MFNNs) with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (MFKANs). Cross-fidelity correlation across the core is weak, making this a challenging multifidelity problem, and neither architecture predicts the transient particularly well in absolute terms. MFKAN nonetheless performs comparably to MFNN for one-time-step-forward prediction while also providing closed-form symbolic equations unavailable with MFNN. To address the scarcity of CFD transients, with only one available per fidelity level, TabDDPM-generated synthetic data was used to augment cross-fidelity forecasting. KAN and FNN achieve comparable self-evaluation accuracy (Pearson correlation of roughly 0.73--0.81), but both perform poorly at true cross-fidelity forecasting (correlations of 0.03--0.06). Assembly-level analysis shows that each assembly's forecast correlation tracks its real cross-fidelity correlation for both architectures ($r=0.840$--$0.896$ for KAN, $r=0.804$--$0.903$ for FNN), confirming that forecasting accuracy is fundamentally limited by how correlated the fidelity levels already are. Overall, KAN-based multifidelity modeling achieves accuracy consistently comparable to MFNN across all settings, while additionally providing symbolic equations that match or exceed the spline representation's accuracy.

title: Bioclimatic optimization for medium density housing in Jakarta transit oriented developments through microclimate simulation
authors: Nicholas Pranata, Gilig Setyo, Justin Hamzah, Farhan Sidqi Purnawan, Irma Desiyana
abstract: Rapid urbanization and the expansion of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) in tropical megacities often overlook the microclimatic experience of pedestrians, leading to severe Urban Heat Island (UHI) effects and thermal discomfort. This study introduces and computationally evaluates the Bioclimatic Transit-Infill Housing (BTIH) concept, a medium-density housing model with minimum parking, located at the Blok A Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station in Jakarta, Indonesia. By reallocating space from parking infrastructure to communal green areas and passive design, the proposed model seeks to improve thermal comfort for last-mile commuters. This study utilized Autodesk Forma to simulate critical microclimate parameters, including sun exposure, wind aerodynamics, and acoustic propagation, cross-referenced with calculated Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) and Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) metrics. Baseline analysis indicated extreme thermal stress (UTCI reaching 39 °C) and stagnant wind velocity (< 1 m/s). Conversely, predictive simulations of the BTIH suggest that subtractive geometric massing optimizes wind flow within the layout. Furthermore, the podium functions as an architectural shading facade, with theoretical WBGT values tracking near 29.45 °C, while acoustic strategies reduced rail noise to below the 55 dB residential threshold. This study, operating within the boundary assumptions and default settings of Autodesk Forma and its calculations, provides an early-stage simulation-based design evaluation rather than a field-validated environmental assessment. By acknowledging that these predictive results are not calibrated against on-site meteorological data or field measurements, this research demonstrates that integrating quantitative building physics into early-stage massing offers a comparative relative framework for localized microclimatic mitigation.

title: Pysammos 1.0.0: a discrete-to-continuum transformation Python tool to analyse the rheology of granular materials
authors: Claudia Elijas-Parra, E. C. P. Breard, John P. Morrissey, P. J. Zrelak, Mark Naylor
abstract: Abstract. Granular flow processes involving different interstitial fluids and coupling regimes are widespread in both natural systems (e.g., landslides, rock avalanches, river sediment transport) and industrial applications (e.g., aggregates in concrete manufacturing, powder technology, animal feed). Despite this, the behaviour of complex granular flows is not fully understood. Modelling of granular media through software packages that couple the Discrete Element Method with Computational Fluid Dynamics (DEM-CFD) enables a comprehensive description of granular small-scale mechanics through simulations of particle-particle and particle-fluid interactions at high temporal and spatial resolution. These approaches are pivotal in the development of constitutive models that represent the bulk rheology of granular media. While DEM-CFD simulations provide particle-scale information (e.g., particle velocities and forces), extracting continuum fields requires a discrete-to-continuum (D2C) transformation that applies a mathematical approach termed coarse-graining. Although some DEM software packages include built-in D2C capabilities, others, such as MFiX-DEM, do not. Consequently, users are often required to develop custom D2C workflows or adapt simulation outputs to the requirements of other D2C tools. Hence, we introduce Pysammos, a Python package that performs discrete-to-continuum transformations and is designed to be user-friendly, open-source, and computationally efficient. Pysammos is able to process polydisperse granular mixtures of any particle shape, while also offering the option to analyse different particle phases separately. It post-processes output files from MFiX-DEM software and produces vtkhdf outputs ready for visualisation in ParaView, as well as a more generic h5 format for further data analysis. Pysammos is able to operate on standard desktop computers as well as on HPC systems. Finally, we showcase a variety of exemplar applications such as sediment erosion, crystals and magma in a conduit, bedload transport and impact cratering.

title: PoreML: A Data-Driven Framework for Learning Multiphase Flow in Porous Media
authors: Chunyang Wang, Mingrui Zhang, Yuyan Zhang, Linqi Zhu, Xin Ju, Edo Sicco Boek, Martin Blunt, Gege Wen
abstract: Multiphase flow in porous microstructures is central to CO$_2$ storage, fuel-cell operation, and flip-chip packaging. Predicting these flows remains challenging because wettability and complex pore geometry govern the nonlinear evolution of fluid interfaces. Machine learning holds substantial promise for advancing the field, but progress is constrained by scarce time-resolved 3D datasets and a lack of a unified workflow for training and evaluating models. To fill this critical gap, we introduce PoreML, an open-source framework unifying data generation, model training, and evaluation grounded in pore-scale physics. The framework comprises three core components. (a) A modern GPU-native lattice Boltzmann solver, validated against analytical solutions and published experiments, enables reproducible data generation. (b) A 3.3 TB dataset contains 560 simulation runs and 158,546 stored time steps across four application-driven scenarios. These trajectories span synthetic structures and geometries derived from micro-CT scans of real materials, covering diverse wetting conditions and viscosity ratios. (c) A unified learning framework evaluates one-step prediction and autoregressive rollouts. Its domain-specific evaluation protocols assess predictive accuracy and physical consistency. We evaluate five models of diverse architecture under these protocols. Two complementary challenges assess transfer to larger domains and from synthetic to micro-CT-derived structures. PoreML provides a shared foundation for machine-learning research on multiphase flow in porous media, with the aim of empowering the community to develop reliable predictive models and advance the field.

title: Online Learning of a Spectral Eddy Viscosity Closure for Large Eddy Simulation Using Ensemble Kalman Inversion
authors: K. Kostova, Yi-Fei Guan
abstract: Large Eddy Simulation (LES) resolves only the large, energy-containing structures of turbulent flows while modeling the effects of unresolved subgrid scales. As a result, the ac- curacy of LES strongly depends on the subgrid-scale closure. This work investigates the online calibration of a spectral viscosity closure for forced two-dimensional turbulence using ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI). The closure consists of a wavenumber-dependent viscosity function, which is parameterized by a 16-dimensional vector. An ensemble of potential parameter vec- tors is passed through coarse resolution LES simulations, and the resulting kinetic energy spec- tra are compared with a DNS reference spectrum up to the LES-resolved wavenumber range. Then, ensemble statistics iteratively update the spectral viscosity parameters in order to reduce the model-data discrepancy. The convergence of the spectral mismatch is used to assess the accuracy of the calibrated closure by comparing LES with the filtered DNS data in spectral space. The results demonstrate the potential of EKI-based online calibration as a derivative- free framework for constructing data-driven turbulence closures with multiple parameters.
